activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
The codon chart was taped to the back wall of Lab 3, laminated and curling at the corners, and Sophie had been avoiding it for twenty minutes. Mr. Reyes had split the class into pairs for the DNA unit's final practical: given a strand of messenger RNA, build the corresponding protein, amino acid by amino acid, and defend your work at the end of the period. Her partner Marcus wanted the top score badly, partly because his brother had gotten one last year and nobody in his family had let it go since. Sophie wanted something harder to name, which annoyed her, because she usually liked naming things.

She read the mRNA strand aloud, sliding her finger along the paper. "A-U-G, then G-U-U, then G-U-C." She copied the triplets into her lab notebook, triple-checking each one, because last week she had transposed a U and an A and the whole exercise collapsed. "AUG is methionine," Marcus said, flipping through his notes. "That's the start. Write methionine." He said it the way you announce the opening move of a game you intend to win.

GUU gave them valine. They matched it against the chart together, Marcus holding the notebook while Sophie pressed the paper flat. But when she looked up GUC, she stopped. "This says valine too." Marcus leaned in, saturnine behind the safety glasses he hadn't bothered to take off. "You read it wrong." "I don't think I did." She traced the chart with her pen. GUU and GUC, side by side, both pointing to the same amino acid, like two doors into the same room.

"That can't be right," Marcus said. "It's a code. Codes don't repeat." He believed this with the fervor of someone whose whole strategy for biology class had been treating it like a substitution cipher, one letter swapped for another, neat and closed. Sophie had been using the same heuristic, she realized, and it had never failed her until now. She counted the codons on the chart, all of them, ticking with her pen while Marcus protested that they didn't have time. There were sixty-four.

"So wait," Marcus said. He flipped to the back of the textbook, where the table of amino acids was printed. Sophie counted those too, twice, because the number looked wrong. Twenty. Sixty-four possible codons, twenty amino acids. "So most of these have more than one codon," she said slowly. "Valine has GUU, GUC, GUA, GUG. It's not a mistake." Marcus stared at the chart as if it had personally insulted him, and Sophie watched him do the thing she had done a minute earlier, which was to suspect the chart before suspecting his own assumption.

He tried to argue it was a printing error, and when that failed, he suggested they use only the first codon they'd found for valine and ignore the second, so the answer would look clean. "It's read in codons of three bases," he said, tapping AUG, G-U-U, G-U-C. "Fine. But we write one valine and we don't mention the other one." Sophie understood the appeal; a clean answer felt like a correct answer, and she'd been confusing the two for most of the semester. But the second codon was sitting right there in their strand, doing exactly what the chart said it did, and pretending otherwise would be a kind of lie with a lab notebook as witness.

"Mr. Reyes is going to ask us to defend it," she said. "If he asks why there are two codons for valine and we say we don't know, that's honest. If we hide one, that's not a different answer, it's the same answer with something deleted." Marcus exhaled through his nose. His brother's perfect score sat between them like a third lab partner. Then, at the end, when Mr. Reyes stopped at their bench and asked about the double valine, it was Marcus who answered. "Most amino acids have more than one codon," he said, flat, almost sullen. "Sixty-four codons, twenty amino acids. It's redundant." He said redundant the way you say a fact that exonerates the chart and convicts your own certainty.

Sophie wrote their final sequence on the board, methionine, valine, valine, threonine, and stood back. Somewhere in the translation between RNA and protein, the cell had solved the same problem she was holding, redundancy as design rather than sloppiness, though she couldn't say yet why it worked that way and wasn't going to pretend she could. Mr. Reyes hadn't told them, and she hadn't asked, because she wanted to get there herself. Marcus was already eyeing the next pair's board, comparing their sequence to his own. "They wrote alanine," he murmured. "For G-C-U." Sophie looked at the chart. GCU was alanine. She looked again. So was GCC, and GCA, and GCG, and there were more beyond that, waiting in the laminated square on the wall. "Marcus," she said, "come look at this."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
Laura sat on the warped wooden bench at the edge of the playground, nominally watching her little brother, actually rereading the magazine she had swiped from the dentist's waiting room that morning. Between an article about sleep and a quiz about friendship, there was a paragraph about the psychologist John Gottman, who distinguished a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character. She read it twice, then folded the page down, because in four days her team had a tournament and she, as captain, was supposed to tell Maya what nobody wanted to tell Maya.

The problem had a history. Maya was brilliant on her feet, quick with rebuttals, funny in cross-examination, and she had missed practice twice the week before midterms and shown up late on Saturday with her case file still in her backpack. Priya had cornered her afterward and said, in front of everyone, "You always mess up, you never take this seriously," and Maya had gone very still, the way she did, and then left through the gym's side door. Since then the team had split into two grim little factions, almost sectarian in their loyalty, Priya's group not speaking to Maya's group, everyone speaking through Laura.

Her brother came off the slide and demanded a push on the swings, and she pushed him while she thought. What she kept circling was the difference between the two sentences. "You missed practice twice" was a fact about what Maya had done; "you always mess up" was a verdict on what Maya was. Laura had felt the difference herself last spring, when a coach had told her she was lazy, and she had carried the word around for weeks like a stone in her shoe. She could still remember the exact day it stopped hurting, and she remembered that nothing about her behavior had changed, only that a different coach had said her footwork needed fixing, and she had fixed it.

But she wasn't sure the distinction was enough. Honesty still had to be honest. Maya's lateness had cost them a real practice round, and Priya's anger wasn't invented, and if Laura softened everything into kindness she would be lying by omission, which was its own kind of disrespect. She tried to imagine the sentence she would actually say, and every version sounded either like a peroration, some formal captain's speech that would make Maya defensive before Laura finished the first clause, or like a craven apology for having an opinion at all.

Then Maya herself walked across the playground, backpack over one shoulder, having texted Laura an hour ago to ask if she was here. Laura's stomach tightened as though the air around the swing set had ionized before a storm. Her brother, oblivious, kept chanting higher, higher.

"I talked to Priya," Maya said, sitting on the neighboring swing without moving it. "She says if I'm at Saturday, we're fine, but if I'm late again she's asking Ms. Okafor to reassign partners."

"Are you going to be late?"

"My mom works Saturdays now. I have to take my brother to my grandmother's first. It's the bus, it's two buses." Maya looked at the wood chips. "I didn't say that at practice because everyone was already yelling."

"Here's what I should have said," Laura said, "Saturday, when it happened, instead of just standing there. You missed practice twice, and it messed up our mock round, and I was frustrated. That's it. That's the whole thing. What Priya said wasn't that. What Priya said was about you, like you're a person who doesn't care, and that's not true, and it wasn't fair." She heard herself stop, and let it be stopped.

Maya was quiet, drawing her sneakers back and forth through the wood chips. "You're the first person who said the actual thing that happened instead of the thing about my character."

"Then here's the part that's still a problem," Laura said. "You didn't tell us about the buses. You let everyone decide you didn't care, because it was easier than explaining. I would have driven you. I can drive you." She hadn't known she was going to say that until she said it, and she couldn't tell yet whether it was generosity or bribery, whether she was solving the problem or just making herself feel better about being captain. That part she would have to watch.

"Six-thirty Saturday?"

"Six-thirty," Laura said, and pushed her brother's swing again, higher, as Maya wrote the time on her hand.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Victor had signed up to be a peer health educator because the application said the training counted for forty hours of community service, and because Priya Raman had signed up too, and because, in a smaller voice he did not examine, he wanted to know the things the training promised to teach. Now he sat in the waiting room of the Fenwick Street Clinic with a laminated packet on his knees, a poster of a Pacific archipelago on the wall across from him, each island labeled in small print he kept almost reading and then abandoning. Behind the reception window, phones rang and were answered in the clinic's particular dialect, warm and brisk at once.

A nurse named Dolores collected him at quarter past four. "You're the student who wants to shadow," she said, not quite a question, and led him through a hallway of pamphlet racks. She stopped at one and pulled three brochures, laying them face up on the counter like cards. "Friday you'll present to the tenth graders at Holloway. Consent, contraception, where to get tested. Today we rehearse."

They sat in an examination room with the door open. Dolores explained the format: he would talk, she would play a teenager, and she would be, in her words, "the teenager nobody wants in the front row." Victor opened the packet. The consent section he could already do in his sleep; he had made Priya drill him over video call, both of them laughing until the laughter wore off and the words settled into something serious. Say what you want, hear what they want, either of you can stop it, every time. He ran through it now, and Dolores nodded without applause, which he understood was its own kind of passing grade.

The contraception section went worse. She interrupted him twice, once to say condoms were free where, and once to ask, in a bored teenager's flattened voice, what he thought about people who said the pill made you gain weight. He fumbled the second one, over-qualified, backtracked, finally said he would rather give her the pamphlet and the clinic's number than pretend to be a doctor, and Dolores's shoulders dropped half an inch. "Good," she said. "That's the actual job."

Then she folded her arms and delivered the question he would remember. "I feel fine," she said. "Why would I get tested?"

Victor's mouth was already open with something about being responsible, and he heard how it would land, how it would sound like a poster and not like an answer. He looked down at the packet instead. Somewhere in the third brochure's fine print was the sentence he needed, and he found it and read it silently, twice, before he lifted his head. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms," he said. "So testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." Saying it aloud, he understood it for the first time as an argument rather than a statistic. Feeling fine was not evidence. It was just a feeling.

Dolores held the bored pose a moment longer, then let it go. "Better," she said. "Say it just like that. Don't dress it up."

In the corridor afterward, they passed an infant exam room where a young couple waited with a baby who had been born, according to the chart clipped outside, with a congenital heart condition; the father was pacing, and the mother rocked the stroller with one foot while filling out a form. Victor watched them until Dolores touched his elbow. On Friday he would stand in front of thirty tenth graders, some of whom already thought they knew everything, some of whom knew nothing, most of whom would look at him the way he had once looked at health teachers, which was to say through them. He would be the one instantiating the whole idea of the clinic in a single person, a volunteer in a polo shirt, the difference between a fact heard and a fact kept.

He texted Priya from the bus: I think I can actually do this. Then, before sending, he deleted actually, and sat with the version that remained, which was both truer and less certain. Outside the window the streets ran on toward Holloway, toward Friday, and a woman two seats away was reading a pregnancy test's instruction sheet with her coat still on.

He got off two stops early and walked.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
The assignment had seemed harmless on Monday: a ten-minute play drawn from your own life, table read on Friday, staged the week after. By Wednesday Aaron had written four pages about a night in eighth grade when he had lied to his mother about where he was, and by Thursday he had rewritten it twice and hated both versions with an epicurean attention to detail, savoring each flaw like a bad olive. The play was called "The Porch." On the porch in question, a boy named Danny tells his mother he is sleeping at a friend's house and then does not. Everything else was still negotiable.

"Whose porch is it actually?" Priya asked him in the cafeteria, stealing his fries with the ease of someone who had long stopped asking. "Like, in real life."

"My grandma's. But I gave it to the mom in the play because the mom needed somewhere to stand."

"That's cold. Stealing a porch from your grandmother."

"She's a misanthrope, she doesn't use it. She sits inside and watches Judge Judy and complains about the neighbors' hedge."

Priya pointed a fry at him. "That's your play. Forget the lying. Write the grandma."

"She's not in the play."

"She's in your life, and the assignment is your life." She said it the way people say obvious things, which was annoying because it worked on him immediately.

Friday, the drama room had been rearranged into a rough circle of chairs, scripts on knees, and Mr. Okafor, who taught the class like a man permanently amused by his own students, clapped twice and said, "Table read. Seated read-through, no staging, just to hear the dialogue out loud before we touch any blocking." He said it every time, the way a priest says the responses, and Aaron had heard it so often it had stopped being words. Until it was his script on other people's knees.

He had cast himself as the mother, which he'd thought was funny, and Tyler, who was built like a rower and read everything in the same flat delivery, as Danny. Priya had claimed the stage directions and was performing them with inappropriate drama, turning "Danny looks away" into a whole physical tragedy. And then Tyler read the line. "I cannot tell you where I am going tonight, Mother, because the truth would disappoint you deeply."

The room went quiet in a way that transfixed Aaron, not with admiration but with the pure social horror of it. Somebody laughed. Mr. Okafor did not laugh, which was worse.

"That's the line," Aaron said. "That's literally what I said to her."

"Nobody says that," said Marisol from the far side of the circle. "Nobody says 'the truth would disappoint you deeply' unless they're a Victorian ghost."

"That's what I meant, though. That's the true version."

"Then the true version is a Victorian ghost," Tyler said, still flat, and the room broke up, and Mr. Okafor raised one hand to settle it and said only, "Notice what the table read is for. Now you know. Revise."

So that was the lesson, delivered by chairs and paper and Tyler's deadpan mouth: you couldn't hear your own dialogue in your head, because in your head it was still attached to you, warm and defended. Spoken aloud by a rower who didn't care, it came out as costume. Aaron sat with this through lunch, through chem, through the walk home, and found it branching into something larger that he couldn't quite close his hand around. It was about lying, obviously; the play was about a lie, and the play itself had become a lie, a smooth false line standing where a clumsy true one should be. But it was also about his grandmother's porch, which he had stolen because it staged better, and his grandmother herself, whom he had cut because she was difficult. Priya wanted difficulty in the play. He wanted shape. Both of them were maybe right, and he could not see how.

He rewrote Thursday night. The line became "I'm at Josh's, I already told you," which is what he had actually said, a small flat lie that his mother had accepted with a nod that he still thought about. He put the grandmother in. He put the hedge in. He cut his favorite monologue, which hurt, and which he suspected was the point, or a point, or at least adjacent to one.

The following Friday they read the revision, and the line landed so quietly that nobody laughed and one person leaned forward, and Priya read the final stage direction, "Danny stays on the porch a long time," with no drama at all, which somehow was the drama. Mr. Okafor closed his copy of the script and said, "That one's yours. Both of them were, but that one's the one you can stand behind."

After class, Marisol caught him in the hallway with his pages under his arm. "Good revision. Are you going to stage the grandma or cut her for the performance?"

"Stage her. She's the best part now."

"Your real grandmother know you put her in a play?"

"She'll find out when she buys a ticket."

"She buys tickets?"

"No," Aaron said, "she thinks the school theater is a waste of a gym. But if I get famous she'll come, and she'll complain the whole time, and that's how I'll know it worked."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so a Seder or a Sabbath dinner is held on the evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it.
story:
The message from the synagogue office arrived on Tuesday, and Alexander read it three times before he understood what it said. He had signed the community hall rental form for Saturday night, which he had assumed was the night of the family Seder, because the calendar on his phone marked Passover on Saturday. Mr. Reiss's note was brief: the holiday starts Friday at sundown, so Saturday night was the wrong evening entirely, and another family had the hall for Friday. Alexander sat at his kitchen counter with the form in front of him and felt the floor tilt a little. His grandmother had handed him the whole Seder this year, the shopping and the cooking and the running of it, because her hands had begun to shake when she lifted the roasting pan, and he had said yes too quickly to consider what yes contained.

He called his cousin Maya first, because Maya was the one who traveled and would be gone by Sunday. "I have to move everything to Friday night," he told her. "The holiday begins at sundown, so the Seder is the evening that starts it, not the evening that ends it." Maya was quiet for a second, then said, "So my 7 a.m. flight Saturday still works," and he wrote that down. His uncle would need to leave work early. His aunt, who ran a bakery and was something of an epicure about matzo ball soup, would need to bake Thursday instead of Friday, and when he called her she sighed the sigh of a woman rearranging ovens in her head.

The hall remained the problem. He went there in person on Wednesday, stood at the little front desk under the fluorescent light, and asked the custodian, a man named Felix with a ring of keys on his belt, whether anything could be done. Felix flipped through the binder slowly, which seemed to presage a no. "Friday you've got the Bernstein thing at eight," he said. "But they only booked the big room. The little room's free from five." Alexander did the arithmetic out loud: sundown was around 7:40, which gave him two hours and forty minutes in the small room before the Bernsteins needed the lobby. His family had never needed more than the corner of Grandmother's kitchen anyway.

Thursday he cooked, and the cooking was its own kind of argument. Grandmother's recipe cards were written in her sister's handwriting from 1968 and assumed a cook who already knew everything, so Alexander found himself calling her between steps, holding the phone against his shoulder while he salted the brisket. "Don't crowd it," she said, and, later, "More than you think." He wanted to follow the cards exactly, as if fidelity to the recipe were a way of keeping her at the table, and at the same time he wanted to adjust, because his little cousin couldn't eat onions and the soup needed adapting. In the end he split the difference, one pot traditional and one pot altered, and wrote a note about it on a paper towel so he would remember which was which.

Friday afternoon he arrived at the hall early with his father and the folding tables. The small room smelled of floor wax and someone else's party. They set twelve places, and Alexander placed the Seder plate in the center and checked it twice, the shank bone, the egg, the bitter herb, the charoset he had made the night before and tasted until it stopped being his grandmother's and started being his. Maya arrived with her suitcase already packed for the morning flight. His aunt came with a foil-covered pot in each hand and looked at the room with an expression he could not fully read.

At 7:40 the light through the high windows had gone the color of weak tea, and Alexander stood up. He had the Haggadahs in a stack, his grandmother's old one on top with its cracked spine, and he realized that everyone was looking at him and no one was going to tell him when to begin. He poured the first cup himself, badly, sloshing a little over the rim, and heard his uncle say, "Nice form," which got a laugh and loosened something in the room. He began the way the book began, and his voice sounded steadier than he felt.

The middle of the Seder he ran his own way. He asked the youngest the four questions as tradition required, and then he did something his grandmother had never done: he opened the floor, asking each person at the table to name one thing that had felt like slavery and one thing that had felt like leaving it this year. His cousin talked about a job she'd quit. His father, surprising him, talked about a friendship he had let go cold for eleven years and had finally called in March. His aunt, the soup judge, said "This charoset is better than mine," and then looked briefly as though she regretted admitting it, and Alexander wrote nothing down because some things you trust yourself to remember.

Somewhere in the second cup, Felix knocked once and pointed at his watch, and Alexander nodded and picked up the pace without letting it show. They ate quickly but not carelessly, the brisket sliced a little thicker than his grandmother's and pronounced good anyway, and by the time the Bernsteins' guests began drifting through the lobby, his family was on the afikoman, the hidden matzo his little cousin had found under the stage curtain and ransomed back for five dollars.

When the room had emptied and the tables were folded, Alexander stood alone by the door with the trash bag in his hand. He did not know whether the Seder had been good in the way his grandmother would have measured good, and he understood that he would not get to know, that this was the kind of thing you never get graded on, only invited back to do again. His grandmother was waiting by the car with her coat buttoned wrong at the bottom. He started toward her with the bag, and before he could say anything she said, "Next year you do the soup from scratch."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Transport costs shrink the gains from comparative advantage, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays.
story:
The quiz came back with a red circle around question four, and William had gotten it wrong twice now, once in class and once on paper. Why do both countries gain from trade? He had written that each one makes what it is best at, and Mr. Okafor had marked it and written one word in the margin: "Closer." Closer, but not there. The retake was Thursday, and William did not want to walk into it with an answer that was only almost right.

He was still turning it over after last period when he found Priya and Dan in the courtyard behind the gym, hunched over a folding table with a pitcher and a hand-lettered sign. LEMONADE, TWO DOLLARS. They were raising money for the robotics club, and they had eleven days to make four hundred dollars.

"Where'd you get the lemons?" William asked.

"Foodtown," Dan said. "Three dollars a bag."

"There's a produce market on Delancey," Priya said. "Eighty cents a bag. My aunt shops there. But it's across town."

William did the arithmetic out loud, half to them and half to himself. Three dollars against eighty cents. Two dollars and twenty cents saved on every bag. Then he asked how they would get there, and Dan said the bus, and the bus was two seventy-five each way, and Priya said that didn't matter because they'd buy a whole crate, enough for the whole week.

At the Foodtown they squeezed a bag of lemons into maybe fourteen cups, which at two dollars a cup meant each bag brought in twenty-eight dollars against three spent. On Delancey, Priya's aunt had said, the same bag cost eighty cents. William wrote the numbers in the margin of his quiz, below the red circle, and drew a line between them. One person was better at making lemonade cheaply and one place was better at making lemons cheaply, and the gap between them was where the money lived. He felt a small exhilaration, the kind that came with seeing a shape inside a shape, and he almost said something about how this was exactly the thing on his quiz.

Then he tried to parametrize it, the way Mr. Okafor was always telling them to do, put the numbers in a general form and see what held. Let the bus fare climb. Let the gap shrink. He ran his pencil down the page and stopped. If it cost one person more to carry the lemons across town than the difference between what lemons cost in the two places, the whole arrangement collapsed. Two seventy-five times two was five fifty in bus fare, against two twenty saved per bag. They would need to buy three bags just to break even, and they didn't have a way to carry three bags, and they didn't have a fridge to keep them in.

"So it's not worth it," Priya said when he showed her.

"It's worth it if we buy enough," Dan said.

"We can't buy enough. That's the point. The bus eats it."

William sat back. Here was the thing, he realized, that question four had been circling. Both sides still gained from trading, that part was true, he could feel it was true, the Delancey grower and the robotics club both came out ahead if the goods moved. But the gains were not a fixed prize. They shrank as the carrying got expensive, and somewhere past a line, the trade simply stopped paying. His first answer hadn't been wrong so much as incomplete, and Mr. Okafor's "closer" now looked less like a rebuke than a map.

He took the retake on Thursday and wrote it plainly: each one gains by making the thing it gives up least to make, and both sides gain even if one is better at everything, but only so long as the cost of moving the goods doesn't exceed the difference in what they cost to make. Mr. Okafor read it while William stood there, then looked up.

"Where'd you finally get it?"

"Lemonade stand," William said. "Bus fare across town."

Mr. Okafor laughed once and wrote something at the top of the page. He turned it around so William could see the check mark, and beside it, underlined: comparative advantage.

Priya texted him that afternoon. Sold out at lunch, she wrote. Still buying lemons at Foodtown. William slid the phone into his pocket and walked out past the folding table, where Dan was stacking the last cups into a pyramid, two dollars at a time.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
Brayden's board was titled "Pushed Around: Equilibrium Under Temperature Stress," and the second word had been misspelled on the bus, corrected in the parking lot, and now sat slightly crooked above two beakers of pink solution. The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and someone else's vinegar volcano, which had already erupted twice at table nine. He had chosen cobalt chloride because it changed color, pink when the equilibrium favored the hydrated form, blue when it tipped the other way, and because color was the kind of thing a judge could see from three feet away without reading a single paragraph of his abstract.

Priya Fernando was two tables down with a wind tunnel and a laser. She wanted the regional slot, the one that came with a banner and a photograph in the local paper, and she had told him so in October with the courtesy of someone announcing weather. They had been friendly in the way of two people who keep score. She came over now with her badge already pinned straight and studied his beakers.

"Which one is hot?" she said.

"This one. The pink turns blue when I warm it, and back when it cools." He lifted the hot beaker by its rim, set it in the ice bath he had rigged from a cooler and a bag of pellets, and they both watched the blue creep back toward rose along the bottom of the glass. It looked, he thought, like a tide deciding against the shore.

Priya frowned at it. "That's not a fair test. You're changing two things."

"I'm changing one thing."

"You're changing temperature and color."

"The color is the measurement. The temperature is the cause." He heard his own voice get defensive and adjusted it. "The reaction sits at an equilibrium, and when you heat it, the system shifts to use up the added heat. Cool it, and it shifts back the other way. It pushes against whatever you do to it."

"So it's stubborn."

"It's more like it's balanced and trying to stay that way."

Priya picked up his reference list, which was half a page, typed the night before. "Who's Chatelier?"

"Le Chatelier." He had typed the name from the panel that morning. The chemistry department had borrowed three displays from the science museum in the city, and one of them stood at the end of their aisle, a tall panel about equilibrium with a portrait of a bearded man. Brayden had looked him up on his phone in the hallway. "The principle is named after Henry Louis Le Chatelier," he said. "He was a French chemist. He stated it in 1884." The date had stuck with him, the way certain dates do, because it meant the idea was older than the gymnasium, older than the town, and had been waiting patiently all that time for him to misuse it.

He had misused it once already, that morning, in practice. He had put a beaker in the warm bath and declared, to his lab partner Marcus, that the reaction would speed up. Marcus, who considered himself a connoisseur of Brayden's failures and kept a private catalogue of them, had pointed out that speed and direction were different claims. Brayden had started to remonstrate, saying that obviously heat did both, and then stopped, because it obviously did both, and the interesting question was which part the principle was actually about. It was about the shift. Not faster, but elsewhere. He had rewritten his conclusion twice on the bus.

A judge arrived at eleven, a woman with a lanyard and an Igneous Rock Club tote bag, which Brayden noticed and decided not to mention. She dipped a thermometer into his warm bath, asked him to run the cold trial again, and watched the color turn without expression. Then she asked him something he had not prepared for: whether the principle told him anything about the world outside the beakers. She said it lightly, the way judges ask impossible questions when they are deciding between two good projects.

Brayden looked down the aisle at the museum panel, at the Frenchman's photograph with its fixed, patient stare. "It tells you systems push back," he said. "But it doesn't tell you how far, or how fast, or when you've pushed too hard and broken something instead of shifting it. I don't know where that line is." The judge wrote something. She might have been writing "honest." She might have been writing "should have had a second trial."

Priya came back during cleanup, while he was dumping the pink solution into the waste jug and the ice had melted into gray water. "They took my wind tunnel data to ask about turbulence models," she said. "Your beakers turned a nice color." She paused, straightening a poster corner that did not need straightening. "I still want the banner, though."

"I know," Brayden said. He held up the last beaker, still faintly blue at the rim where his hands had warmed it, and set it down in the ice water to watch it change.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
The lab room smelled of the exhaust fan's old dust, and Violet sat with her worksheet flat under the fluorescent light, the equilibrium problem refusing to open for her. CoCl4 squared off against CoCl6 in the equation, and the question wanted to know what happened when the temperature dropped. She had been fine with concentration changes all week, shifting the balance one way or another like adding weight to a scale, but temperature had no arrow in the equation, no term she could push. It sat outside the reaction like weather outside a window, and she could not get her hand on it.

Across the bench, Marcus was already drawing something, his pencil moving with the confidence she had envied since September. He had finished the practice set before anyone else and now worked ahead into the chapter's last problems, the ones Mr. Okafor would not collect. Violet watched him write the word heat on the right side of his equation, plain as a product, and then add a plus sign in front of it.

"What did you just do," she said.

He turned the notebook so she could see. "For exothermic ones, heat is a product. So it goes on that side." He tapped the arrow, then wrote it again on the endothermic example, this time on the left, among the reactants. "It's just a way of thinking about it. It's not really a chemical."

Violet copied it into her own notes, and the problem changed shape in her hands. If heat was a product of the forward reaction, then lowering the temperature meant taking that product away, and the system would have to make more of it to replace what was lost. The answer unfolded along the cold blue to warm pink line the demo had shown last week, the flask shifting color in Mr. Okafor's hands. She wrote the prediction down and sat back, almost annoyed at how easy it had become, one word penciled onto a page.

She thought of her grandfather then, unbidden. Two summers ago, before he moved into the home, she had sat at his kitchen table while he tinkered with a stubborn hot water heater, explaining to nobody in particular that a system pushes back against whatever you do to it. She had been sixteen and restless and had barely listened, scrolling her phone while he talked about furnaces and pipes, and the memory arrived now with a small weight attached, the particular weight of a kindness she had let pass unanswered. It was not the same thing he had been describing. It was probably not even close. But the gesture of it, the leaning back, the resistance, felt like his.

"You look like you solved something," Marcus said.

"I stole your trick." She turned the notebook back toward him. "Is that allowed? Writing heat in like it's a thing?"

"It's a model," Marcus said, with the slight superiority of someone who had read the sidebar text twice. "It works for predicting. Whether it's true is a different question."

That distinction sat with her through the rest of the period. She tested the trick against the remaining problems and it held every time, exothermic heat on the right, endothermic heat on the left, temperature changes falling into place like the concentration changes she already trusted. Still, a small unease remained, a feeling that she had borrowed a way of seeing without knowing where it broke. She remembered her mother disenfranchising the whole idea of pre-calculus once, saying the teacher's graphing tricks never survived the real exam, and how that cynicism had turned out to be wrong, and how some other cynicism that year had turned out right. You could not always tell in advance which skepticism to keep.

When the bell rang, Mr. Okafor stopped her at the door, not to check the worksheet, only to say that her grandfather had called the school office last week asking whether she still did the science fair. She said she wasn't sure. The subterranean current of that answer, the ennui that had settled over her ambitions sometime between junior year and now, was something she had not named to anyone, and she did not name it now. She said she'd think about it, and he nodded and let her go.

In the hallway she found Marcus at the water fountain and told him about the hot water heater, the old man with his tools, the way he had talked about systems pushing back. "Maybe that's why it stuck," she said. "Maybe I already half knew it and just needed the words on the page." Marcus said something about how memory worked like that, and she let the claim stand without agreeing to it. She looked down at her notebook, at the small penciled word she had added to a stranger's equation, then closed the cover and walked with him toward the buses, the late sun striking the lockers at a low angle through the corridor's tall windows.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
The hostel's courtyard smelled of orange peel and rain, and Brayden had exactly four days to become someone who could argue about climate policy in Spanish for five minutes. His sister, Maya, had signed them both up for the intercambio night at the cultural center without asking, the way she did most things, and when he'd protested she'd said, "You took four years of Spanish, Brayden. Use it or it dies." Now he sat with a laminated list of energy vocabulary, repeating transición, renovable, impuesto, while she fed crumbs to the courtyard's putative cat, an animal that belonged to no one and everyone.

His partner for the debate was a local student named Teo, who was seventeen and spoke English only when he wanted to be funny. "Tu acento," Teo said on the second evening, tilting his head, "es como un gringo cantando." Brayden laughed, but the laugh sat wrong in his chest afterward, and he lay awake composing sentences he would never have the nerve to say. Their opponent, according to the sign-up sheet, was a university student named Rocío, who had won the regional competition in the spring. Teo delivered this information with the flatness that seemed to portend disaster.

On the third day they practiced in the plaza, under the plane trees, and Brayden discovered that his problem was not vocabulary but structure. In English he could argue circles around anyone; his father called it the family disease. In Spanish, each sentence cost him something, and halfway through a point he would forget the clause he'd begun. "Empieza otra vez," Teo kept saying, "pero más simple," and Brayden resisted this, because simple felt like surrender, until Maya, watering the plants beside them, said quietly, "Simple isn't dumb. It's clear." He watched her steady the small pot she'd bought the hostel's owner that morning, the woman whose knees had been aching on the stairs, and he let the sentence go and started over with three plain words instead of twelve.

Rocío turned out to be formidable in a way he hadn't imagined. At the informal session on Thursday she spoke on carbon taxation with such fluency that he understood maybe two-thirds and felt the shape of the rest, the way you feel a wave through a boat's hull. Afterward she approached their table, and Teo, nervous, made a joke of it. "Él va a debatir contigo," he said, and then, in English, with a grin that didn't quite reach his eyes, "Good luck understanding him." Rocío looked at Brayden and waited. Brayden understood the joke, and understood also that it had been aimed somewhere uncomfortable inside him. "Vamos a ver," he said, and was pleased at how steady it came out.

The debate was Saturday evening, folding chairs in a room with tall windows, maybe thirty people. Brayden opened with the argument he'd rebuilt a dozen times, that a carbon tax works fastest when its revenue returns to households, and he got through ninety seconds before his grammar began to fray. He slowed down. He let the pauses exist. Somewhere in the fourth minute, when he'd said that the tax without rebates punishes the people with the fewest choices, Rocío responded, and he understood every word: she didn't answer the point. She said, smiling at the audience, that it was charming to hear a foreigner pronounce economía that way, and the room laughed, a small warm ripple at his expense.

For a moment the laughter filled his ears and he nearly lost the thread of everything, the Spanish, the argument, the room. Then he remembered a term from Mr. Alvarez's class junior year, surfacing the way forgotten things do, whole and intact. He raised his hand for the moderator. "Un momento," he said. "Eso es un ad hominem. Ataca a la persona, no al argumento." His accent made the Latin words sound strange, but the moderator, an older man in a gray cardigan, nodded slowly, and some murmur went through the chairs, and Brayden realized he had just done, out loud and in two languages, the thing the whole fallacy meant: he had named the attack on the person instead of the claim, and named it as a fallacy, the way it is treated in formal debate. Rocío's smile thinned. She returned to the rebates, and they fought over the actual point, and it was hard, and he lost the thread twice and found it twice.

When the five minutes ended he was sweating through his shirt. He couldn't tell who had won, and the moderator, when asked, said only that the audience would decide what it had heard. Brayden found this unsatisfying and then, walking out, less so. He had walked in with an argument he'd sanded down to what he could actually defend, and he'd discovered, mid-sentence, a distinction he'd previously known only as a vocabulary word: attacking a person is not answering them, and it doesn't count as answering them here, either. Whether his own position survived the evening was another question, one he turned over on the walk back, and he noticed he liked the turning.

Teo bought churros from the cart by the fountain and handed Brayden the first one without comment. Rocío appeared at the edge of the lamplight, backpack over one shoulder, hesitating. She came over and said, in Spanish, that his pronunciation of impuesto had been wrong all night, and that his argument about the rebates had been, if he wanted honesty, half right. "Which half?" Brayden asked. She tore a piece off her own churro and considered him. "Come back Tuesday," she said, "and lose to me properly, and maybe you find out."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole.
story:
Mia set the bag of table salt on the kitchen scale and watched the numbers flicker before they settled. 585 grams. The science fair was in nine days, and her project was supposed to test whether different salt concentrations slowed the growth of bacteria on kitchen sponges. Her poster board was already lettered, but the poster was decoration; the experiment was the part that would be judged, and she could not start it until she knew how much salt to measure out per beaker.

Her chemistry teacher had gone over molar mass in October, while Mia was still half-distracted by cross country practice and the noise of the radiator. She remembered fragments. A mole, whatever it was, sat somewhere between a number and a unit, and you needed the molar mass to get there from grams. She had assumed the details would amortize themselves across the semester, that paying attention in installments would eventually cover the whole debt. That had not happened. Now the debt was due.

She cleared the counter of cereal bowls and her brother's skateboard magazines and spread out her notes. Sodium chloride, she read, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole. She said it aloud once, to the empty kitchen, the way she used to memorize times tables in third grade. "Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole." The window over the sink held the gray light of four o'clock, and the sponge she planned to use for the trial sat beside the faucet like a small exhausted animal.

Her grandmother came in for tea, moving slowly, still in her coat. She had been a nurse for forty years, and when she glanced at Mia's notes, her face changed. "Moles," she said. "We used that word in the hospital pharmacy. Saline solutions. Nobody ever told me what it meant, they just taught us the recipe." She filled the kettle. "I got in trouble once for asking."

"Trouble?" Mia asked.

"A supervisor said, you don't need to know that, you need to know that the bag is labeled correctly. I thought that was backwards." Her grandmother poured hot water over the tea bag and sat down across from Mia. "Knowing why the number is what it is, or at least knowing the number itself, that seemed like the difference between doing a job and understanding it."

Mia looked down at the page. She had been treating the calculation like a locked door, something she would need permission or a key from someone else. But her grandmother had spent a career on the far side of that door, following recipes without the reasons, and it had bothered her for forty years. That made the door feel less official, somehow. Less like a gate and more like a gap in a fence that people climbed all the time.

She picked up her pencil. If sodium chloride has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole, she reasoned, then a mole of it must weigh 58.44 grams, which meant the bag in front of her, at 585 grams, held ten moles and a little more. She checked the arithmetic twice, dividing 585 by 58.44, and got 10.006. She turned the paper so her grandmother could see. "So if I want a tenth of a mole per liter, I weigh out 5.844 grams."

Her grandmother leaned over, still holding her tea. "And that would be the same in every hospital in the country."

"Everywhere," Mia said. "That's the point, I think. It doesn't depend on the scale or the bag or the country." She was not entirely sure that was the point; she still could not have said what a mole actually counted, only what it weighed in salt, and she could feel the shape of that missing piece like a stair not taken in the dark. But the beakers did not need her to know everything. They needed 5.844 grams, dissolved, measured.

She tore a paper towel, folded it, and zeroed the scale with it. Then she opened the bag and began pouring, slowly, the white grains sliding out in a thin stream while she watched the display climb toward the number. Her grandmother reached over and steadied the bowl with one hand.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
Daniel had spread the textbook across the picnic table so that both pages faced the sky, and he was copying the diagram onto a paper bag because he had left his notebook in Marcus's car. The diagram showed glucose being broken down, first in the cytoplasm, then inside the mitochondria, where the carbon pieces spun through a circle of arrows that fed electrons into a chain and pushed protons across a membrane. ATP came out at the end like water from a tap. Marcus sat on the table's edge, half on and half off, the way he sat when he wanted to seem like he wasn't really studying.

"You actually want to do this?" Marcus said. "It's Saturday. It's June. We graduated."

"I failed the exam," Daniel said. "I want to understand it before I have to take it again in the fall."

Marcus rolled a bottle cap along the boards with his thumb. He had passed, barely, and the difference between them had become a thing neither of them named out loud. Daniel drew the circle of arrows again, slower this time, and noticed that the first compound in the circle wasn't glucose or anything shaped like it. It was citrate. A six-carbon acid, like the sour stuff in lemons.

"Why is it called the citric acid cycle?" Marcus asked, leaning over. "It's in a textbook. Shouldn't it be called something about energy or cells?"

Daniel didn't know. He flipped back through the chapter and found a name in the caption, small print under the diagram. Hans Krebs. He read it aloud. "Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937." Below it, in even smaller print, something about a prize. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it."

"So a guy just found it and got his name on it," Marcus said. "Like a planet."

"It's not his name on it, though. It's the acid. His name is in the caption." Daniel thought about that for a moment. Somewhere in England, in 1937, a man had watched carbon atoms move in a circle and understood what nobody else had understood, and then a committee in Stockholm, sixteen years later, had decided it mattered enough to hang a medal on. Daniel felt the gravitas of it, the weight of a whole life spent on one wheel of reactions, and it made his paper bag diagram seem either ridiculous or connected to something enormous. He couldn't decide which.

He tried tracing the steps out loud. Glucose splits in the cytoplasm, two smaller pieces slip into the mitochondria, the pieces lose their carbons one at a time around the circle, and every turn hands electrons to the chain, which uses them to build ATP. It came out flat, like reciting a pledge. Marcus frowned at the drawing and pointed at the circle. "So the pieces go around once and they're done?"

"They go around and they're gone. Each turn eats one piece." Daniel stopped. That was the part he'd gotten wrong on the exam, or one of the parts. He had written that glucose itself entered the cycle directly, that the whole sugar spun around, and the grader's red line had cut through his answer like a fence. He could still feel the peevish little jolt he'd had reading that mark, the impulse to argue with the paper itself. Now, in the backyard, with the wasps circling the lemonade and Marcus's knee bouncing against the table leg, he saw his error plainly. Glucose never entered the circle. It was taken apart on the doorstep and handed in piece by piece.

"Okay," Marcus said, "but who cares about the names? The exam's not going to ask who Krebs is."

"That's not why I'm reading it." Daniel tapped the caption. "Somebody had to figure this out. It wasn't just sitting in a textbook waiting. He described it in 1937, with Johnson, and then the prize didn't come until 1953. Sixteen years later. Sixteen years of doing the work before anyone decided it counted." He wasn't sure why that steadied him, but it did. His own failure was two weeks old and already felt permanent; here was a man who had needed sixteen years for the world to catch up to what he already knew.

Marcus turned the bottle cap over with his finger. "So you're saying fail slow."

"I'm saying I don't know yet." Daniel picked up the pencil again. "I understand the steps now, mostly. I still don't really get how moving protons makes ATP, and I can't tell if I'm getting it or just memorizing it again in a prettier order. That's the part I can't fix by tonight." He said it without the shame he'd expected to feel, and that absence assuaged something in him more thoroughly than any pep talk from his mother had managed.

He redrew the circle one last time, then wrote the date 1937 next to it in the margin, small, where a grader wouldn't see it but he would. Then he folded the paper bag along its creases, the way it had been before, glucose to citrate to the little turbine of the membrane, and pressed it flat under his hand.

"Quiz me," Marcus said.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
story:
I was not nervous about the critique, which is why I had rewritten it four times. The art program at Camp Wrenhaven had eleven of us, a box of prints from the museum in the city, and a final presentation on the last Friday that counted for the scholarship letter. My counselor, Dara, had said the letter mattered, so I decided it did not matter to me at all, and I told everyone at the picnic table so.

I had chosen Frida Kahlo's The Broken Column because it looked hard and I wanted to look hard too. My first draft was three pages on composition, the vertical seam splitting the figure, the desert horizon, the coral band of the dress. I used the word "juxtaposition" six times. My roommate, Priya, read it with the flashlight after lights-out and said it was like being lectured by a very serious vending machine. I told her formal analysis was supposed to be doctrinaire, that was the whole point, and she said she didn't think that word meant what I thought it meant.

The problem was the eyes. I had written, with total confidence, that Kahlo looks away from the viewer, down and inward, grief turned private. I remembered it that way. I would have sworn to it in front of a judge. But when I unrolled the print in the craft cabin on Thursday to practice, Kahlo was looking straight at me. Not near me, not past me. At me, the way the lifeguard looks at you when you've drifted past the ropes.

"Nails," Priya said over my shoulder. She was eating a granola bar meant for the hike. "They go through her face and her whole body. And she's crying. Full tears, both cheeks."

"I know," I said, which was a lie, and she knew it was a lie, and I knew she knew, so I just said it louder. "I know."

The trouble with the eyes was that they were mine. I was crying. Not dramatically, just enough that I could malign the humidity, the pine pollen, the general camp atmosphere of dust and adolescence. Priya handed me the granola bar wrapper to dab with, which was disgusting and kind, and I thought about how I had spent three pages explaining the seam down the middle of the painting without once saying why a person would put herself back together like that in front of an audience.

Priya's own critique was on a Monet, all soft boats and forgiving light, and she was doing it partly to avoid exactly what had happened to me, and I maligned her for it, out loud, and she took it well because she is a better person than I generally admit. "You can't critique something you're scared of," she said. "You can only flatter it or run." That was the closest thing to wisdom anyone gave me all summer, and she delivered it while extracting a splinter from her palm.

So I started over, and the starting-over was mostly sitting. I sat in front of the print for forty minutes while the other campers played capture the flag and someone's whistle shrieked at intervals through the trees. I had been treating the painting like a math problem with a right answer, and there was a version of me that wanted to keep doing that, that wanted the scholarship letter so badly I could feel it in my back teeth. But you cannot be doctrinaire about a person staring out at you while nails pierce her face and body and tears run down her cheeks. Or you can, but then you have written about the seam and the coral and nothing else, and you have missed the entire reason the painting exists, which is that she refuses to look away even while she is being taken apart.

On Friday I stood up with the print and no pages, because I had left my notes in the dining hall on purpose, or possibly by accident, and I am still deciding which. I talked about the color first, the green against the raw umber of the desert, how the greens don't soothe anything, they just frame the wound. Then the composition, the vertical column, the sheet held in one hand like a curtain she could raise or lower and chooses, for whatever reason, not to. Then I said the thing about the gaze. "She's crying," I said, "and the nails go right through her face and body, and still she looks straight at you, and I find that almost impossible to look back at, and I think the discomfort is the point." Dara asked how we could formalize discomfort, and I said I wasn't sure we entirely could, and eleven people went quiet in the way that means either you've done it or you've embarrassed yourself permanently.

I did not win the presentation, is the honest part. A boy named Theo won, with a very clean analysis of a Vermeer that involved actual geometry and zero tears, and his scholarship letter will be better than mine, probably, or at least tidier. Dara told me afterward that mine was the one she'd remember, which is the kind of thing adults say, though she said it looking at the print and not at me, which made it more believable. On the bus home Priya slept against the window and I held the rolled-up reproduction in my lap like something breakable, and when I unrolled a corner of it in the tunnel of highway trees, Kahlo was still looking straight at me, patient as ever, not asking to be understood, only seen.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
Austin had chosen the back corner of the library because it was the only place where talking was permitted, though barely, and because the shelves there formed a kind of booth that hid him from anyone who might wander past. On the table in front of him lay a photocopied Spanish news article, three short paragraphs about a flood, and beside it a sign-up sheet with his name written in the second slot. The oral reassessment was in twenty minutes. If he summarised the article aloud without mistakes, the department would let him skip the intro language course in the fall and go straight into the intermediate one, which mattered to him more than he had admitted to anyone, including himself.

Priya sat across from him with her own copy, the same flood, the same three paragraphs. She had already done her reassessment that morning, fourth slot, and she had come back to the library with an expression he could not read, which frightened him. He had asked how it went. She had said, "Fine, mostly," and turned a page. That equivocal answer had been sitting in his chest ever since, because Priya was better at Spanish than he was. She had taken it since middle school. If the assessment had gone badly for her, it could go badly for anyone.

"Read it again," she said, "out loud, all the way through, then close your eyes and give me the summary."

He read. The Spanish came slowly at first, the consonants bunching up in his mouth, and then it smoothed out the way a path smooths out when you walk it twice. A river had risen. Roads were closed. Hundreds of people had left their homes. When he finished, he closed his eyes and began, in Spanish, "The article reports that heavy rain caused flooding in," and then he stopped, because he could not remember the name of the town.

"It says it right at the top," Priya said.

"There's no town in the first paragraph. It starts with the rain."

"No. Before the first sentence. Those two words in capitals at the very beginning, before anything else starts. Didn't you look at those?"

He opened his eyes. There, ahead of the first sentence, in capitals, sat the name of a city, followed by a dash and then the article's opening words. He had read straight past it a dozen times, treating it like a stain on the page, decoration, part of the newspaper's furniture. He had been so careful with the verbs that he had never once asked what that fragment was doing there.

"That's where the story was reported from," Priya said. "That's what my guy called the dateline, when he marked my sheet."

"My guy," Austin said. "What did he mark?"

She turned her paper toward him. In red at the top, beside a score that was lower than she needed, the grader had written a single line: wrong country in summary. She had told the assessor the flood had happened in the capital, because the capital was the only place name she could find in the text, mentioned once, deep in the third paragraph, as the destination of some displaced families. She had skipped the two words in capitals at the top and invented a geography the article never claimed. Austin stared at the red ink and felt his whole understanding of the task rearrange itself, quietly and completely. All the vocabulary he had drilled, all the physiology of reading, his eyes trained to leap from verb to verb, had trained him to leap right over the one detail that anchored everything else.

"So it's not decoration," he said.

"It's the ground floor, apparently," Priya said. "And I built the whole house in the wrong yard."

He worked through it again, this time reading the way a stranger would, letting the capitals come first. The city in the dateline was not the capital; it was a mid-sized river town he had never heard of, and once he held it in mind, the article's shape changed. The rain was local. The closed roads were those roads. The families moving to the capital were leaving that place, not stranded in it. His summary, when he tried it aloud again, came out steadier than any version he had produced all week, because it finally stood on something. What he still could not tell, and said so, was whether the reassessment would want the dateline spoken in Spanish or left as a proper noun, and Priya shrugged, because she did not know either, and her grader had not thought to say.

The clock over the reference desk showed five minutes to the hour. Austin picked up the article, folded it along the third paragraph so only the top was visible, and stood. He walked toward the front of the library with the folded page in his hand, mouthing the name of the city once more under his breath, and at the door he turned back to Priya and pointed at the capitals.

"Watch the top," he said.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The machine arrived in a box that had clearly been opened and resealed, because Dad never ordered anything he didn't research first, and this one he had researched for two weeks. He set it on the kitchen table next to the salt shaker he was trying to ignore, and Tyler watched him slide his arm into the cuff the way the pamphlet showed, quiet and almost formal, like a man being fitted for something.

"You do it," Dad said. "I keep flinching when it squeezes."

Tyler pressed the button and the cuff hissed and tightened and then let go, and the screen showed two numbers, one over the other. 148 over 94. Dad looked at the ceiling and did the thing he did when he was deciding whether to be worried or just tired, and Tyler, who wanted to help but didn't know how yet, said, "Is that bad?" which was not a useful question and Dad didn't answer it, which was its own kind of answer.

The doctor's office was where Tyler went looking, or rather the folder from the doctor's office, which Dad had left on the counter with his reading glasses on top like a paperweight. Inside was a printout with the 2017 guideline from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association on it. Tyler read it twice, because the first time the numbers didn't mean anything to him. Normal, it said, for an adult, is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. He said the words out loud to the empty kitchen to make them stick. "Normal is below 120 over 80." Below both. He copied it into his phone.

He started reading at the table that night, while Dad watched a game with the sound low. There was a lot about systolic and diastolic, the top number and the bottom number, and a lot less about what to actually do, which was mostly the same sentence wearing different coats: move more, eat differently, cut the sodium. Tyler had assumed, before this, that blood pressure was the kind of thing you either had or didn't have, like a limp. Reading disabused him of that by the second page. It was more like a bank account, and Dad had been making small withdrawals for years without the balance ever being called in.

The trouble was Dad himself, who treated every change like an accusation. When Tyler came home with a bag of unsalted almonds and left it on the counter, Dad ate a handful out of spite and then said they tasted like drywall. When Tyler suggested a walk after dinner, Dad said his knees were between him and the sidewalk, which was true about the knees and not true about the reason.

Tyler tried another way, which was to stop presenting solutions and start asking questions. He showed Dad the guideline printout and pointed at the line he'd copied into his phone. "Under 120 and under 80," he said. "That's the whole target. Both numbers."

"That's for normal people," Dad said, but he looked at the numbers longer than he needed to, and later that week he let Tyler take his reading before the game instead of after, and it was 141 over 89, and Dad said, "Lower than Tuesday," with the careful flatness of a man trying not to be pleased.

The garden was where they ended up, because it was movement that didn't announce itself as movement. Dad had let the tomato bed go weedy since August, and the soil had gone friable and soft with rot under the leaves, crumbling when Tyler dug his fingers in, and the two of them spent a Saturday pulling it apart and turning it over. Dad's knees complained and Dad complained, and Tyler carried the heavy bag of compost without being asked. It wasn't restitution exactly, though Tyler thought of it that way, the way he thought of the almonds and the walks, small deposits against a debt he hadn't incurred, being paid anyway because that was how family worked, or how he wanted it to.

Afterward they sat on the back steps with their elbows on their knees, and Dad's face was flushed and his breathing was loud, and Tyler took the machine outside and cuffed Dad's arm right there on the steps. The cuff squeezed in the cold air, and the screen blinked while it thought, and Dad watched it over Tyler's shoulder, and neither of them said anything until the numbers came up.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine.
story:
The farmers' market opened at eight, and by half past Tristan had sold four jars of his mother's plum jam and memorized none of the vocabulary spread across his lap. He was supposed to be watching the cash box while his mother fetched change from the car, but the exam was Monday, and Monday did not care that Saturdays belonged to the stall.

"Portugal and wine," he said under his breath, tracing a column of his notes with one finger. "Or was it Portugal and cloth." He had written Ricardo's example down twice in class and both times the countries had swapped goods on him, the waydreams rearranged rooms.

"You're muttering at jam," said Priya, sliding around the corner of the stall with two coffees. She handed him one without being asked, which was the kind of thing she did, and which he had never properly thanked her for. She was in the same class, bound for the same exam, and she had a way of standing beside him on Saturday mornings as if it were coincidence.

"It's Ricardo," Tristan said. "There's this original example, England and Portugal, cloth and wine, from 1817, and I keep getting which country had which good backwards. I think Portugal made the wine. That part at least feels safe. England making cloth."

"Feels safe," Priya repeated, and her mouth did the thing it did when she knew something he didn't. She sat down on the overturned crate they used for the honey display and sipped her coffee, unhurried, letting him stew.

He thought of his uncle last spring, before any of this, standing in this same spot and arguing with a man selling goat cheese. Tristan had been fourteen and had asked, later, why his uncle bothered, since the cheese man clearly wasn't going to change his mind about the parking situation downtown. His uncle had said that arguing with someone you'll see every week isn't about winning, it's about keeping the argument alive so the relationship doesn't die of politeness. Tristan hadn't understood it then. He thought of Priya on the crate now, keeping something alive, and understood it a little.

"Fine," he said. "Tell me."

"I'm not telling you. That's not learning, that's copying." She set her cup down. "But I'll trade you. You explain comparative advantage to me, out loud, like I'm a customer, and I'll tell you if you've got the countries wrong."

So he stood up behind the stall, in the same spot his uncle had argued from, and did it as a pitch. Suppose, he said, two countries, and one of them is better at making everything, absolutely better, both goods, and the other one is worse at both. His hands moved over the jam jars like they were England and Portugal. Everyone assumes the strong country has nothing to gain, he said, but the point of comparative advantage was that trade isn't about who's best, it's about what each side gives up least to get what it wants. Even the weaker country has something worth trading, because the strong country's talent is wasted on the thing it's only slightly better at. Both sides walk away ahead. Nobody loses.

"Both sides," Priya said slowly, and he could see her testing it, turning it over the way he had at midnight with the textbook open and the lamp too bright. "That's the part I keep refusing to believe. It sounds like symbiosis, but between countries, like neither one has to lose for the other to gain." She frowned at the jam. "Okay. Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. England and Portugal. Cloth and wine. And you have it right, Portugal is wine, England is cloth." She pointed her cup at him. "You had it right the whole time. You just didn't trust it."

At that moment an obstreperous toddler two stalls down lunged at a display of peaches, and his mother, rushing past with the cash bag, detoured to catch the basket before it fell, and the peach farmer called out his thanks, and for a second the whole market seemed to be a web of small rescues nobody had planned. Tristan looked at all of it, the trades and the rescues and Priya deciding not to simply tell him the answer, and felt the idea settle somewhere deeper than his notes.

"I was going to fail that question," he said.

"No, you weren't," Priya said. "You were going to get it right and then panic and change it." She picked up his textbook, closed it, and slid it under the cash box, out of reach. "That's why I came over. Your mom texted me." She stood and brushed off her jeans, then paused. "Also, I got the countries backwards on Thursday's quiz, so this was for me too."

"You let me do the whole speech."

"Both sides walk away ahead," she said, and held out her hand for his coffee.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
The quarry had filled with spring rain until it was a rectangle of green-black water, and Cameron stood at its edge holding his phone like a man holding a bird he meant to keep from flying. On the screen was the graph he had been assigned to explain, the one from the observatory on Mauna Loa, carbon dioxide rising and rising across sixty years in a line that climbed like a staircase made of teeth. On Monday he would have to stand up in earth science and explain it, and the graph, and the whole business of greenhouse gases, to a room that included Priya Rao, who had already corrected him twice this semester in a voice that was never unkind and never soft.

Marcus had chosen the quarry for the study session, and Marcus's idea of studying was swimming. He was already treading water ten feet out, calling Cameron's name in the bellicose way of boys who want company more than they want to admit it. Dana sat on a flat rock with her sneakers off, and Tess, who was Dana's cousin and in the same class, crouched at the edge dragging a stick through the pale quarry dust.

"I don't get the sawtooth part," Tess said, before Cameron had even sat down. She drew in the dust, and her drawing did look like the graph, a long jagged climb. "The line goes up, and up, and it wiggles the whole way. If the instruments were any good, wouldn't it be smooth?"

"Probably measurement error," Cameron said. "Old machines, right? Like static." He said it with confidence he did not feel, because he had thought the same thing at midnight, leaning over his phone in bed, and the wiggles had looked like noise to him too. He had a page of notes about greenhouse gases, though, and he started there, because that part he actually understood. Sunlight comes through the air, he said, and the ground warms up and gives off heat of its own, and carbon dioxide and the other gases let the sunlight in but hold some of that heat on its way back out, like a blanket that only works in one direction. Dana nodded along. Tess kept drawing teeth in the dust.

Marcus climbed out, dripping, and shook water off like a dog, and Cameron moved the phone fast to the middle of the rock, out of the splash radius. This turned out to be the first good decision of the afternoon, though he did not know it yet.

"Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle," Marcus said, reading over Cameron's shoulder, because of course he would not go get his towel first. "Why does it do that? Is the carbon dioxide, like, breathing?"

Cameron almost said he didn't know, and that would have been honest, but something about the way Tess was carving the little dips into the dust stopped him. The dips came every year. That was the thing he kept sliding past. Not random static, not old machines. Regular as anything. He held the phone flat on the rock so all four of them could see it, and dragged two fingers apart to enlarge the last ten years, and there it was again, the same tooth shape repeating and repeating, springing down and climbing back, springing down and climbing back. Measurement error did not keep a schedule.

"The wiggles aren't mistakes," he said slowly, still testing it as he said it. "Look how even they are. Same size, every single year, for sixty years."

"Then what makes them?" Tess said.

He stared at the dust where she had drawn her teeth, and then at the trees on the far rim of the quarry, the whole green band of them, oaks and brush running along the limestone edge, and then at his own hands, which had gone cold in a way that had nothing to do with the water. Somewhere in his notes from Monday's class there had been a phrase about plants. He had written it down without reading it, the way you write things at the end of a long class period.

"The Northern Hemisphere," he said. "Think about all the plants up here. All of it, everything that leafs out." He pointed at the tree line above the water. "In spring and summer, when everything's growing, the plants take in carbon dioxide. The whole hemisphere's plants, pulling it in.
