Then in autumn and winter, when the leaves die and decay, they release it back." He looked at the graph again, checking his own logic against the line. Down in the northern summer, up in the northern winter, down and up, and underneath it all the slow climb that never stopped. "The plants are the wiggle. That's why it's so regular. The graph is breathing."

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Tess dragged her stick through her drawing and made it again, slower, and drew little leaf shapes at the bottom of each dip, and Dana said, in the voice of someone deciding whether to believe a thing, "So the zigzag is real. The line is doing two things at once."

"Two things at once," Cameron said. "That's actually the whole assignment." He was talking faster now, the words assembling themselves. "The plants take the carbon dioxide back every year and give it back every year, and they've done that the whole century, and the line climbs anyway. It's like, the breathing is steady, and something else is climbing on top of the breathing." He stopped there, because past that point he wasn't sure yet. He did not know how much of the climb was what, and his notes had numbers he hadn't finished checking, and Monday was coming either way. He said so, out loud, because it seemed better to say it than to have Priya say it for him. Dana nodded like that was the right kind of answer, though with Priya he couldn't be sure.

Marcus, still wet, reached over to point at the top of the curve, and his hand dripped, and the drop landed a half inch from the phone, and Cameron slid the phone into his back pocket, dry, and stood up, and Tess was still drawing leaves at the bottom of every dip, one for every year.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Grandpa Sal's arm until his fingers went blotchy, and Isabella watched the digital display climb, stall, and settle. One sixty-eight over ninety-four. She wrote it in the notebook she'd bought for her pharmacy tech course, and under it she wrote his pulse, and under that she drew a small frowning face, which she immediately crossed out because professionals did not draw frowning faces.

"You look like your mother when she's about to tell me the mower is broken," Grandpa Sal said.

"The mower is broken," Isabella said. "I heard it wheezing from the porch. Kind of like you on the stairs."

He laughed, which turned into a cough, which turned into him waving her off toward the kitchen for a glass of water. This was the third reading she'd taken that week, at his request, after his own doctor had said a number at him and then gotten called away, and he'd come home knowing only that the number had been "not wonderful." Isabella had made a chart. She was a person who made charts. The chart had a row for morning readings, a row for evening, and a column she'd labeled "variables," where she tracked whether he'd had coffee, salt, or an argument with his neighbor about the fence line, which was chronologically reliable, occurring roughly every other day. The chronology of it all was the only tidy thing in the house.

The numbers were not tidy. They sat high across the whole week, and when she flipped back through the pharmacy course module on blood pressure, she found that a reading consistently that high had a name. She read it twice to be sure.

"Grandpa," she said at dinner, spooning sauce onto his plate before her own, "it's called hypertension. That's what the module says. Persistent high readings like yours."

"Hypertension," he repeated, testing it. "Sounds like a Greek philosopher. Sounds like something that should be wearing a toga and judging me."

"It kind of is." She turned her fork over. "The module also says regular aerobic exercise, brisk walking or cycling, on most days, lowers blood pressure in a lot of people. Even people who already have hypertension." She said it carefully, the way she'd say a word she'd just learned in Spanish, half expecting him to correct her pronunciation.

He pushed a meatball around his plate. "I walk. I walk to the mailbox."

"The mailbox is forty feet from the door."

"It's uphill both ways if you're committed."

Isabella put her fork down. She thought about her accounting elective, where the teacher had made them amortize a loan across five years so they could see how a big intimidating number became small survivable payments. The word had stuck with her because it felt like a general principle of the universe, or at least of Tuesdays. She drew a line down a fresh notebook page and wrote "week 1" at the top of the first narrow column, then "week 2," then enough weeks to reach September. Under week one she wrote "20 minutes, easy pace, after dinner." Under week two, "25 minutes." The plan was deliberately parsimonious, nothing fancy, no gym, no equipment, just him and the road past the cemetery, which he claimed had the best sunset in the county and which she suspected he'd avoided for six years, since Grandma Rosa.

"Every evening," she said, sliding the notebook across the table. "Most days, the module said. You pick the nights off. Two a week, maximum."

He looked at the schedule for a long time. "And you'll be where during this?"

"Walking with you," she said. "Obviously. Somebody has to carry you home."

He snorted. He signed the bottom of the page the way he signed contracts with the fence guy, with a flourish and a mutter. That night she took his reading again, out of curiosity, and wrote it down without comment: 166 over 92, which she already understood proved nothing, one way or the other, and which she wrote down anyway.

They started the next evening. He set the pace, which was slower than her brisk and faster than his mailbox, and he talked the whole first mile, mostly about the fence, some about the mower, once about a girl he'd known before Rosa and immediately retracted. On Thursday it rained and he wanted to skip, and she stood in the doorway holding both jackets until he surrendered. On Saturday they went twice as far as planned because the sunset was, in fact, ridiculous over the cemetery, and he stood at the gate a while, not saying anything, and she looked at the road instead of at him.

At the end of the second week she pumped up the cuff again in his kitchen, the chart open beside the machine. The display thought about it, the way it did, then gave its verdict. She looked at the number, then at the week's column, then back.

"Sixteen points down," she said. "If that's right."

"It's right enough," Grandpa Sal said, and held out his arm. "Again. I want to watch it happen."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
The robotics lab smelled like solder and cold pizza, and Ryder had been staring at the same line of code for ten minutes when Devon kicked the leg of the workbench and said, "This is garbage, by the way. Your whole teleop branch is garbage."

Ryder looked up. Devon was holding the printout of the drive-team roster, but he wasn't looking at it; he was looking at Marcus, who sat in the corner soldering a motor mount with the resigned posture of someone who had learned not to argue back. Marcus had missed the build deadline on Saturday. He'd said he'd have the arm assembly done and he hadn't, and now Devon was orbiting the lab saying things like "some people just don't care" and "I guess we'll lose at regionals, whatever," loud enough that everyone metabolized the resentment slowly, all afternoon, without anyone naming it.

"That's not helping," Ryder said, finally.

"I'm being honest," Devon said. "You want me to lie?"

Ryder wanted a lot of things. He wanted the arm assembly finished. He wanted Devon to stop doing this corrosive loop every time something went wrong, because the vitriolic version of honesty, he was beginning to suspect, wasn't honesty at all, it was just anger wearing honesty's clothes. But mostly he wanted Marcus to still want to be on the team in three weeks, and that seemed, at the moment, genuinely in doubt.

That night he lay on his bed with his phone and searched, half embarrassed, "how to give feedback without being a jerk." Most of it was junk. One page, though, was from something called the Center for Creative Leadership, and it laid out a model: situation, behavior, impact. You named when it happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. No verdicts on character. No "you're lazy." Just "Saturday, the arm assembly didn't arrive, and we lost the practice day." It felt almost too simple, like a recipe with three ingredients, and Ryder distrested how clean it was. But it also reminded him of something from programming, the modularity of good code, each function doing one thing, taking clear inputs, returning clear outputs. Maybe feedback could work like that too. He wasn't sure. He turned the idea over for another hour before he slept.

The next day he caught Marcus in the hallway outside the cafeteria, before he could talk himself out of it. "Can I say something about Saturday?"

Marcus shifted his backpack. "Devon already said plenty."

"I'm not Devon." Ryder's palms were damp, which seemed absurd, since he was about to say something reasonable to a person he liked. "It's this thing I found. It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model. You just say when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had." He heard his own voice, flat, reciting, and winced. "Okay, that sounded like a worksheet. But here. On Saturday, the arm assembly wasn't finished when the build day ended, and we lost our only practice window before regionals. That's it. That's all I wanted to say."

Marcus was quiet long enough that Ryder began composing his apology. Then Marcus said, "My mom was in the hospital Friday night. I didn't tell anyone because I didn't want it to be an excuse."

"I'm sorry. Is she okay?"

"She's home now." Marcus looked at the floor. "I should have texted somebody. I just went quiet instead."

"You could tell the team that," Ryder said. "Not as an excuse. Just so we know." And then, because the model had one thing it couldn't do, he added, "I don't actually know if saying it the clean way makes it easier to hear. You tell me."

Marcus half smiled. "It was easier than 'some people don't care.'"

At the afternoon build session, Ryder watched Devon launch into his orbit again, and he cut across it, voice steadier than he felt. "Devon. Situation, behavior, impact. Try it." Devon stared at him like he'd started speaking Icelandic, so Ryder said the whole thing himself, the Saturday, the assembly, the lost practice, and then Marcus, unprompted, said, "My mom was in the hospital. I should have told someone. I'll have the arm done by Thursday." The lab went still in a different way than usual, the absence of the low static everyone had gotten used to.

Devon picked up a wrench and didn't say sorry, but he also didn't say "whatever," and when Marcus's soldering iron slipped a few minutes later, Devon just steadied the motor mount with two fingers and held it there until the joint cooled. Ryder still didn't know if three clean sentences could survive a whole season, or whether Devon would ever learn to say them himself, but Thursday was two days away and the arm was half-built and everyone was still in the room.

"Hand me the wire strippers," Marcus said.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and old sweat, and the twelve eleven-year-olds in front of Brianna were already obstreperous, bouncing balls off each other's backs while she tried to pin her practice plan to the clipboard. She had drawn the drills the night before at her kitchen table: three-line passing, weave, chest pass to the target. Her problem was specific and she could name it. These kids telegraphed everything and threw passes that arrived at chests, at elbows, at the backs of heads. Nobody caught anything cleanly.

"Lines," she called. "Five passes down, five back."

It went badly. Every time a pass sailed wide, she corrected the thrower the way her own coaches had corrected her: "Bend your wrists." "Follow through." "Square your hips." The words came out of her mouth like an inheritance, a patrimony of commands she had never thought to question, and the kids' shoulders got stiffer with each one. By the second drill, Marisol, their best player, was staring at her own hands before every pass as if they belonged to a stranger.

Brianna called water and stood alone at the free throw line. She was flashing back, without meaning to, to her junior year, the state semifinal, when Coach Ruiz had told her during a timeout to stop thinking about her elbow. "Stop aiming your elbow," he'd said, exasperated, "aim at the rim." She had made the next shot and the one after that. At the time she'd thought he was just fed up with her. She'd never wondered whether the words themselves had done something.

While the kids drank, she scrolled her phone one-handed, because she had a term paper due on motor learning and a half-formed suspicion. She found the study she'd skimmed a week ago, work by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, and read it properly this time standing on the line with her thumb moving fast. Learners usually improved faster when they were told to focus on the effect of a movement, on the target, rather than on their own body parts. She read it twice. Her whole coaching vocabulary, it turned out, had been pointed the wrong direction, at wrists and hips instead of at the thing the wrists and hips were for.

She set the phone down on the bleachers. It could exhilarate a person, this feeling of a door swinging open, and it could also sting, because every correction she'd given tonight had made somebody worse.

"New rule," she said when they came back. "I'm not going to talk about your bodies anymore. Not your wrists, not your feet. Listen for what the pass does, not what you do."

Marisol squinted at her. "Then what do we think about?"

"Hit your teammate's hands," Brianna said. "That's it. The pass has to arrive at their hands. Don't think about how."

They ran it. The first five minutes were chaos, because the kids kept glancing at her for the old instructions, and Brianna had to bite down on every correction that rose in her throat. When Devone's pass smacked Marcus in the shoulder, she said only, "Hands, Devone," and stepped back. The second five minutes were different. Passes began to arrive where hands were waiting. Marisol caught three in a row without looking down, and Marcus, the worst passer on the team, threw one that hit Marisol's palm so cleanly that she gasped.

"Again," Brianna said, and they went again.

At the end of practice she had them run the weave one last time, and it was better, it was unmistakably better, balls snapping hand to hand down the floor. But it wasn't fixed. Devone still threw high when he got excited, and half of them would probably forget by Thursday, and Brianna understood that she'd traded something away, too. The old commands had made her feel like a coach, somebody with technical authority; this new way made her more like a witness, standing quiet at the edge while they found the target themselves. She wasn't sure yet which of those she was supposed to be.

The last kids filed out. Marisol lingered by the door with a ball under her arm.

"Same thing Thursday?" she asked.

"Same thing," Brianna said, and began collecting the cones.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
The kettle had just begun to sigh when Isabelle spread the printout across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the curling corners with a salt cellar and a jar of marmalade. The graph showed carbon dioxide climbing in a jagged line from the 1960s to now, and beside it, in her own handwriting, the notes from the online course she had started two weeks ago: parts per million, Keeling curve, wavelength. Her grandfather set down two cups and looked at the paper the way he looked at weather coming in over the ridge, without comment.

"Can I ask you something," she said. "About the graph."

He sat, folded his hands, and waited. He was a laconic man, her grandfather; whole visits could pass on a dozen words, and Isabelle had learned that his silences were not indifference but attention, held open like a door.

She traced the line with one finger. "So this is carbon dioxide, measured every year, and it goes up and up. It never dips, not really. Even the little wiggles are just seasons." She glanced up. "That's what I'm supposed to be able to explain by Friday. How the gases trap heat. How to read this."

"There were men who worked the quarry," he said at last. "My father among them. They'd have looked at that and seen their livings in it, one way or another." He tapped the paper's edge, where she had written the source in small print. "Who made this?"

"Some observatory. I wrote it down. Mauna Loa, and then ice cores for the older part." She was proud of having recorded the provenance of every number, because her teacher had drilled it into them that a graph without a source was just a shape. "That part I understand. What I don't understand is the argument I got into yesterday."

There was a knock at the back door and Theo let himself in, as he always did, shaking rain off his jacket. Theo lived three farms over and had driven Isabelle's mother crazy since they were both seven. He pulled out a chair without being asked and read the graph upside down with the ease of someone who did everything sideways.

"Still fighting with Dev," Isabelle said, "from chemistry."

"The quarry kid," Theo said. He grinned. "You know what's funny, people stigmatize the kids whose dads work there, like they personally dug the hole in the sky. Dev's dad hauls stone, that's all." He reached for a biscuit. "What's the fight?"

"He says if you want to slow warming in the next few years, you go after methane leaks first, not carbon dioxide. I said that's backwards, because everyone says carbon dioxide is the main problem, it's the one in all the graphs, it's the one we measure at Mauna Loa." She flattened the paper. "He got mad. I got madder."

Her grandfather sipped his tea and said nothing, which Isabelle had come to understand as permission to keep going.

"So last night I looked up methane, and here's the thing." She pulled a second sheet from her folder, covered in her cramped notes. "A methane molecule traps far more heat than a carbon dioxide molecule. Way more, per molecule. I thought Dev had that wrong and he didn't." She paused. "But it only stays up there about a decade on average. Carbon dioxide stays much, much longer. Centuries, some of it."

"So who wins the argument?" Theo asked.

"That's what I couldn't figure out. Both, I think. Or neither." She turned her cup slowly on its saucer. "If a gas disappears in ten years and a different one stays for centuries, then cutting the short-lived one changes things faster, but cutting the long-lived one matters more for, like, everything after us. Dev was arguing about the next few years and I was arguing about the whole century, and we were both talking as if it was one question."

Her grandfather rose, refilled the kettle, and set it back on the stove. When he turned around he said, "Your grandmother settled arguments like that by feeding people."

"I'm not wrong, though," Isabelle said. "Am I? About carbon dioxide being the long one?"

"You're not wrong," he said. "That's not the same as winning."

Theo snorted into his tea. Isabelle looked at the two graphs side by side, the century's slow climb and the methane notes beneath it, and something settled in her, not a conclusion exactly but a willingness to hold both lines at once. She took out her phone and typed a message to Dev: "You were right about methane being stronger per molecule and shorter lived, about a decade. I was arguing a different timescale. Talk tomorrow?" She set the phone face down before the reply could come or not come, because she wasn't ready to know which.

The kettle began to whistle. Her grandfather lifted it off and poured, and Isabelle moved the marmalade jar so the steam wouldn't wrinkle the paper, pressing the graph flat with the heel of her hand as though she could keep the line from climbing any further tonight.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
The trail behind the community college cut through oaks and then opened onto a mown field, and Clara had chosen it because the placement exam was in six days and her bedroom had begun to feel like a held breath. She carried a binder of flashcards and a water bottle and the particular stubbornness of someone who had tested into the lowest tier of everything and was tired of it. Biochemistry was the section she feared most. The words themselves seemed recalcitrant, refusing to arrange themselves into anything she could hold onto: glycolysis, pyruvate, NAD+, the electron transport chain, as if the cell were a factory built in a language she had never been offered.

Her friend Priya had come along, ostensibly to sketch, actually because Priya never believed anyone should study alone. They stopped where the trail widened near the field's edge, and Clara sat on a flat rock and shuffled the cards without looking at them.

"Say one," Clara said.

Priya took the deck. "Okay. Where does glycolysis happen, and what does it start with?"

"Outside the mitochondria. In the cytoplasm. It starts with glucose, one six-carbon sugar, and it breaks it down to pyruvate." She said it fast, the way you say a phone number before you forget it. "And it makes a little ATP. Two net. That's the part I keep losing. Everything after that needs oxygen, but glycolysis doesn't."

"Correct," Priya said, and drew an oak leaf in the margin of her sketchbook.

The problem, as Clara understood it, was that she could memorize the sequence but not the reason anyone should care. The steps enraptured her when she read about them late at night, this tiny combustion happening in every cell of her body, but by morning the enchantment faded and she was left with the same blank page. Her mother said she thought too much and too separately. Her brother said she should just get the tutor the college offered for free. Clara had refused the tutor with a pride she couldn't entirely justify, some conviction that if she couldn't build it herself, in her own head, on her own walk, then it wasn't really hers.

"Last card," Priya said. "What happens to pyruvate when there's no oxygen?"

"I don't know that one yet." Clara stood. "Ask me tomorrow."

"You have six days."

"Then don't waste today's oxygen on worrying." She started across the field at an easy jog, just to move, and Priya's laugh followed her and then thinned out behind her, and then there was only her own breathing.

She sprinted. She didn't plan to; her legs simply wanted to, the way legs do when the grass is short and the far fence is measurable and the afternoon has been sitting too long. Halfway across, her thighs began to burn, a heat that climbed from muscle into certainty, and by the time she reached the fence her legs were shaking and she had to grip the wire and stand there with her head down, gasping. Her lungs felt too small for the request her body was making.

And standing there, bent over, she thought about oxygen. Not in the abstract way of the flashcards but as a shortage, an actual deficit in actual muscle, and she thought: my cells are running low on oxygen right now. This is the scenario. This is the card.

She walked back slowly, turning it over. Glycolysis didn't need oxygen, that much she had. Glycolysis took glucose to pyruvate and made two ATP per glucose, small change but fast, and it needed something else, some partner molecule, NAD+, that had to be there or the whole thing stopped. She remembered the phrase from the textbook, NAD+ regenerated, and she had underlined it twice because the sentence had felt like a lock without a key. The cell, starved of oxygen, still wanted its two ATP. It still wanted glycolysis. So what did it do with the pyruvate?

Her legs ached, and the ache had a name she had heard in gym class years ago without anyone explaining it, lactic acid, and the ache was saying something. Lactate. The muscle made lactate. From what? From pyruvate. When muscle cells run low on oxygen, she thought, they convert pyruvate into lactate.

She stopped in the middle of the field. But why would a cell bother? Making lactate had to cost something, and then the cost resolved itself the way a word resolves itself when you finally hear it spoken: the conversion put NAD+ back. It regenerated NAD+. That was the point. The cell burned pyruvate into lactate not as a failure but as a trade, sacrificing the pyruvate so that NAD+ existed again, so glycolysis could keep running, so the two ATP per glucose kept coming even while she stood here starving every cell of oxygen. Her legs weren't just tired. They were rationing.

She was laughing by the time she reached the rock, breathless and half-doubtful, because she had assembled the whole thing from a burn in her thighs and two underlined sentences, and half-doubtful was a familiar country for her.

"Ask me the last card," she said.

Priya looked up, pencil still. "What happens to pyruvate when there's no oxygen?"

"When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate," Clara said. "And that regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis can continue, making two ATP per glucose." She said it slowly, and then, quieter, testing it: "That's why my legs are burning right now. I sprinted the field to check."

Priya lowered the sketchbook. "You sprinted a field to study?"

"I sprinted a field because I wanted to, and then it turned into studying." Clara sat down on the grass, still catching her breath. "I don't know if I have it exactly right. I don't know everything about it, just that one piece. But I know it from the inside now, from my own legs, and that feels different."

Priya was quiet for a moment, in the way she was quiet when she was deciding whether to say the subtext out loud. "You know the tutor's still there," she said. "If you wanted."

"I know." Clara pulled a blank card from the binder and wrote on it, then turned it so Priya could see: low oxygen, pyruvate, lactate, NAD+, 2 ATP. "But this one's mine. I earned it in the grass."

Priya took the card and added a small drawing in the corner, a stick figure running with burning legs, and handed it back. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Same trail," Clara said, and put the card on top of the deck.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
Grandpa's living room smelled like pencil shavings and instant coffee, which was strange, because Jordan had never seen the man sharpen anything. He had come out here on a Saturday because his environmental science teacher had assigned each student a topic to teach back to the class, and Jordan had drawn "the greenhouse effect and the Keeling curve," which sounded like a magic trick and a Bond villain respectively.

"So you're hiding from homework in my house," Grandpa said, setting down two mugs. "Bold strategy. The refrigerator is a good spot, nobody checks there."

"It's not hiding, it's retreating with dignity." Jordan spread his printout on the kitchen table. The graph showed a line climbing steadily since the fifties, with a jagged edge, like a mountain range drawn by someone impatient. "I have to explain this to thirty people on Monday, and right now I understand it about as well as I understand cricket."

Grandpa put on his glasses upside down, corrected them, and leaned in. "What's the squiggle?"

"That's the actual measurements, I think. The line wobbles up and down each year but keeps undulating upward, like a snake climbing stairs." Jordan turned the graph sideways, hoping a new angle would help. It did not. "The problem is I keep reading that greenhouse gases are bad, and then I keep reading that they're natural. Both can't be true, or one of them is lying, or I'm an idiot."

"Those are three options, yes."

"Thank you for narrowing it down."

At that moment the back door banged and Priya came in, carrying her bike helmet and half a granola bar. She lived two farms over and had appointed herself Jordan's academic supervisor since fourth grade, a position no one had offered her. "The planetarium had a show on the Moon this morning," she announced. "You missed it. It was freezing, visually speaking. Minus 18 degrees Celsius on average, the narrator said, and that's basically Earth without its greenhouse effect. She said our planet would be that cold too, minus 18, instead of the roughly 14 it actually is, if not for the gases. So greenhouse gases are a blanket, not a villain."

Jordan sat up. "Wait. Say the numbers again."

"Minus 18 versus about 14. I wrote it on my hand." She showed him. She had.

"So they're not a bad thing at all," Jordan said slowly. "They're the reason anything can live here."

"Except your graph," Priya said, tapping the printout, "shows we've added a lot more of them lately, and that part's on us. That's the chicanery. The effect itself is innocent. The extra amount, not so much."

"That's like blaming a blanket for the person piling on twelve more."

"A murderous blanket-shopping spree," Priya agreed.

Grandpa raised a finger. "So which one do you tell your class? Good or bad?"

Jordan looked at the graph, at the climbing snake of it, and understood that the honest answer was not a side but a both, held at once: the gases were the reason the Earth was not a frozen rock like the Moon, and they were also the thing being pushed out of balance. "I say the blanket keeps us alive at about 14 degrees, and then I say we're the ones adding layers, and I show them this." He traced the jagged upward line with his pencil. "I don't have to pick a team. I have to explain the graph."

"That'll go over well," Priya said. "People love being told the answer is complicated."

"They'll survive. Like the Earth did, at minus 18, before the blanket." He was testing the sentence, and it worked; he felt it land somewhere visceral, the idea of the whole green planet locked in ice, and then not. He started writing on the back of the printout. Blanket: keeps Earth at roughly 14 Celsius. No blanket: about minus 18. Extra blankets: see graph, apologize later.

"What's the wobbly part called, though?" Priya asked. "Someone will ask."

Jordan checked his notes. "Seasonal cycle, I think. Plants breathe in and out through the year, so the line sawtooths. Don't quote me until I verify it, though. I've been wrong twice already today and it's barely noon."

"Twice?"

"The cricket thing, and the part where I thought retreating with dignity was different from hiding."

Grandpa collected the mugs and paused at the counter. "For what it's worth, in nineteen sixty-two I saw that graph in a magazine and thought it was a picture of a heartbeat. Told your grandmother the world had a pulse." He shrugged. "Turns out I wasn't entirely wrong, just early."

Jordan looked at the line again, the small teeth of it rising and rising, and put his pencil down on the last data point, the newest one, the one nobody had lived in yet.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up.
story:
Brooklyn set out the cups at seven-thirty, before the heat arrived, because she had learned last summer that noon was too late and the customers had already committed to the gas station slushies. The stand was a plywood sheet over two sawhorses, inherited from a yard sale, and the sign said FRESH LEMONADE, $1, with a smaller sign underneath that said TUTORING, ASK BROOKLYN, MATH THROUGH PRECALC. The tutoring was the real business. The lemonade mostly functioned as advertising that a responsible teenager lived at this house.

Her appointment calendar had become the problem. She had eleven students now, four of them prepping for the same placement exam she herself was taking in September, and their parents texted at all hours wanting to move sessions, cancel sessions, add sessions before the test. Brooklyn could answer those texts in under a minute each. She was, by any honest measure, faster at it than anyone she knew, and she did it for free, which is to say she did it at midnight between practice problems on trade and specialization.

Her brother Theo was eleven and had a tablet and a streak of mercenary calm that Brooklyn sometimes mistook for indifference. On Saturday morning he sat on the curb beside the stand, having been promised one dollar per hour and ten cents per scheduled session, and watched her pour.

"You're better at the phone than me," Theo said. This was true and he said it the way he reported weather. "So why am I getting paid."

"That's the question on page twelve," Brooklyn said. She had a stack of index cards on the cash box, because the exam in September included economics and the tutoring paid two hundred a week and the lemonade paid, on a good day, eleven dollars. The card in her hand had a sentence on it she'd underlined twice. She read it out loud, mostly to herself, partly because Theo was the only audience available. "A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up."

Theo chewed on this with the seriousness of a boy who had found money in it. "So I'm the assistant."

"You're the assistant who types slower than me, yes. Congratulations."

The morning produced a trickle of customers: two landscapers who bought two cups each, a jogger who paid with a twenty and told Brooklyn to keep it, which was the discernment joggers seemed to think they alone possessed. Between them a mother arrived with questions about tutoring, and while Brooklyn explained rates and the diagnostic worksheet, Theo fielded three texts without looking up from his game, rescheduling a Tuesday to Thursday and booking a new student whose mother had found the stand through the lemonade, exactly as Brooklyn had planned and would never admit aloud.

The card stack had a phrase on it, comparative advantage, which Brooklyn had initially taken to mean being the best at something, a reading that the morning was quietly dismantling. She was the best at scheduling. She was also the one students' parents were paying forty dollars an hour to see. Every hour she spent typing was an hour of that given up. The logic held its shape even when she prodded it looking for holes, though she did not like everything it implied. It implied, for instance, that Theo should keep getting paid to do something she could do better, and it implied nothing at all about whether that was fair to him, or fair to her, or whether the words "fair" and "gains" were even talking about the same world. The book had nothing to say on that point. The book assumed you wanted the biggest number.

By noon the heat had driven the customers indoors and the pitcher was half gone. Theo had scheduled six sessions, netting himself a dollar and sixty cents, and had asked whether the rate could be renegotiated for August, when the exam prep rush would presage, as Brooklyn put it, either a boom or a collapse of the entire enterprise. Theo asked what presage meant. Brooklyn said it meant what the clouds had been doing since ten o'clock, and then, of course, it started to rain.

They scrambled the umbrella over the stand, the cash box under Brooklyn's arm, the sign inside out, and stood together under the dripping awning while the yard went dark. Theo held out his hand, palm up. On it sat his tablet with a calendar full of names, times, and a note in the Saturday slot that read RAIN, CLOSED, PAID ANYWAY?

Brooklyn looked at the note for a long moment. The specious answer was that she should do it herself and keep the money, since she was faster, since she was better, since she had built the whole thing. She had underlined that sentence twice and she believed it, and it still felt like a cheat, like being talked out of something by a well-dressed argument.

She counted out a dollar and sixty cents, and added a dime for the rain.

"August is negotiable," she said. "Ten cents a session, plus weather."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
Mia had always considered herself the careful one, the one who read past the headline, the one her friends sent things to before reposting them. So when the video appeared in her feed during third period, a hallway full of students screaming, water pouring through classroom doors, a caption reading "our school, this morning," she felt the familiar tightening in her chest that meant she had to do something. She screenshotted it. She typed half a comment. The video had forty thousand shares already, and every share felt like a small door closing, because if she waited, she would be one of the people who waited.

She found Priya in the library at lunch, hunched over a laptop with a sullen set to her mouth that Mia had learned meant she'd been arguing with her brother again. Mia slid into the chair across from her and turned her phone around. "Is this your school?"

Priya glanced at it, then looked again, longer. "No. But it's not yours either."

"You don't know that."

"I know the desks." Priya tapped the screen where a row of chairs stood half submerged. "Your school has the plastic ones with the hole in the backrest. Those are the old wooden kind. My mom teaches at a school with those."

Mia told herself she was checking because she was careful, though a colder, more honest part of her knew she was checking because she wanted Priya to be wrong. She opened a search engine and dragged the video's thumbnail into the image box, the way she'd seen someone demonstrate once in an assembly she'd mostly slept through. The results loaded slowly, the library wifi stuttering, and Mia sat with her thumb hovering over the share button while the little wheel turned.

The first match was a news article from three years ago, and the second was from a country whose alphabet she couldn't read, though the site helpfully transliterated its name into Latin letters below the logo. The same water. The same wooden chairs. The same boy in a yellow raincoat being carried on a teacher's back, an image that had made Mia's throat hurt when she'd believed it happened that morning, forty minutes from her house.

"Some people call it SIFT," Priya said, watching her face. "It stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context." She said it flat, like she was reciting something she'd been made to memorize, and Mia wondered which of Priya's arguments with her brother this had come from.

"You could have led with that," Mia said.

"You could have led with checking before you screenshotted it for me like it was proof."

That stung, and Mia let it sting, because there was truth under it. She had wanted the video to be real, not because she wanted a flood but because a flood near her, a flood at a school like hers, would confirm something she'd been saying for months, that nobody was coming to fix anything for people like them until something dramatic forced them to. A false video didn't make her wrong, exactly. But it didn't make her right, either, and she had been prepared to use it as though it did. She thought of her own finger on the share button, that small gesture, and how complicity probably didn't feel like a decision. It probably felt exactly like this, like urgency, like caring.

The weird part, the part she turned over all through sixth period, was that the flood had happened, just not to them. Real students had waded through that water three years ago, in a town she couldn't pronounce, and their emergency had been recycled into someone's content, stripped of its date and place until it became pure fear, portable and reusable. Whoever had reposted it with the new caption hadn't made anything up. They had only made it useless.

After last period she stood at her locker with the phone in her hand, the video still there, the comment still half typed in the draft box. Down the hall, a group of ninth graders were crowded around someone's screen, one of them saying "our school, this morning," and laughing, and then not laughing. Mia could tell them what she'd found. She could delete the draft. She could send Priya's article to everyone she knew and feel correct for a day. Or she could close the locker and walk out through the parking lot, where the sky had gone the color it went before heavy rain, and let the ninth graders work out for themselves what she had almost not worked out herself.

She typed a reply to one of the comments, then deleted it, then typed it again. Behind her, a teacher's door slammed shut against the wind.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The laundromat on Fairview Avenue had two folding tables, and Liam had claimed the one farther from the door because the nearer one wobbled and because his mother had once balanced a pie on it during a blackout, an act of optimism the whole family still cited as evidence of something. He spread the two leases side by side, weighted the corners with quarters, and began transferring numbers into a notebook while the dryer thumped behind him like a patient heart.

The apartment on Cypress Street was cheaper by forty dollars a month. He had found it first, applied for it first, and liked it in the abstract way you like something you have only seen in photographs. The one on Delancey was forty more but included water and trash, which he had assumed made the comparison simple until he sat down and realized he did not actually know what utilities cost, which was the kind of ignorance that felt different now that it had a deadline attached.

"You're doing homework at a laundromat," said Priya, dropping her basket onto the wobbly table and watching the quarters slide. "This is the saddest thing I've ever seen, and I once watched Mr. Kellerman try to parallel park the golf cart."

"Rent," Liam said. "My mom's moving in with my aunt in March, so I need a place by summer, and it has to be the right place, because wrong means I can't do the program in the fall." He turned the notebook toward her. Two columns. Numbers marching downward like the legs of a declining animal.

Priya picked up the Cypress lease, flipped pages with the indifference of someone who had never had to read one, and stopped at a paragraph near the end. "What's this part? It says you have to show proof of insurance before move-in."

"It's renter's insurance," Liam said slowly, reading over her shoulder, and as he said it the whole clause assembled itself in his mind. "It covers my stuff, not the building. The landlord's policy handles the building. This one's on me, and it's a premium, every month, on top of rent." He sat back. The lease put it in dense language, something about indemnity for the tenant's personal property, but the plain shape of it was simple: another line in his column, one he had not known existed until four seconds ago.

He remembered then, with a small internal wince, the afternoon in October when his aunt had sat at the kitchen table with a folder of her own papers and said, "Read everything, even the boring parts," and sixteen-year-old Liam had said, "It's all boring parts," and gone outside to shoot baskets at the rim with no net. She hadn't lectured him. She had just said, "Okay," and kept reading, and now here he was at a folding table, reading the boring parts like scripture, and he could almost hear her not saying anything at all, which was somehow louder.

He called an agent's office from the sidewalk, coins warm in his palm, and got a number for a basic policy. Twelve dollars a month. It did not sound like much until he added it under Cypress and watched the cheaper apartment stop being cheaper. He stood there a moment in the smell of dryer sheets and cold air, doing the arithmetic again as though repetition were a form of appeal. Cypress plus insurance plus all utilities, against Delancey plus insurance plus everything except electric. Delancey won, but only by nine dollars, and nine dollars felt like a margin thin enough to see through.

Back inside, Priya had read three more pages and was holding one up. "Is any of this germane to your little math problem, or is it just the landlord reserving the right to be difficult?" Her finger rested on a clause about quiet hours.

"Put it in the pile," he said. "Everything's germane now. This lease instantiates the entire concept of fine print." He took the page, folded it into the notebook, and looked at his two columns, which had stopped being numbers and started being a life he was choosing. He had wanted certainty, the satisfaction of a clean answer, and instead he had a nine-dollar difference, a policy he'd only half understood over the phone, and the dawning suspicion that being an adult was mostly this: making the best decision available and then keeping the receipts.

The dryer buzzed. He pulled out his clothes, folded the shirts badly, and slid the Cypress lease into his backpack without throwing it away.

"Delancey?" Priya asked.

"Delancey," he said, "unless something on page eleven ruins my life."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
The community centre had been a church once, and the music room still held the smell of old hymnals even though the piano was a donated Yamaha with a chipped middle C. Naomi arrived early on Thursdays because Mr. Ferreira, who ran the theory class, let the students use the room before the lesson, and she needed the hour. Her scholarship audition was in nine weeks, and the written paper would ask her to mark the form of a Mozart movement: where the exposition ended, where the development began, where the music found its way home.

Her method, so far, had been to count. She made a grid in her notebook, one column for bars, one for keys, one for themes, as if she could operationalize listening, turn it into a procedure that would yield the right answer the way a chemistry lab yielded a result. The first theme appeared in G major, then a second theme in D, and then the opening returned in G again, and she had drawn her brackets accordingly. Exposition, development, recapitulation. She had even colour-coded it.

Devon came in at quarter past, headphones around his neck, carrying the recording he'd borrowed from the library because his phone didn't have space. He was the only other person under fifty in the class, and he was garrulous in a way that filled the room, which Naomi sometimes found comforting and sometimes found exhausting. Today he was following the same movement with the score open on the piano lid.

"Wait," he said, and stopped the recording. "Is this thing broken? The pianist went back. He played all that and then just started over." He scrubbed backward, played it again, and the opening theme came back exactly where he'd said it would, innocent, cheerful, as though nothing had happened.

Naomi leaned over. In the score, at that point, stood two dots stacked like a colon, then a thick double bar. "That's a repeat sign," she said. "In these Classical sonata-form movements the exposition has repeat signs around it, so the performer plays the whole exposition twice before the development begins." It came out flatter than she intended, like reading a label aloud, and she regretted it immediately, because Devon's face did the thing it did when he felt slow.

"So he didn't mess up."

"He did what was written."

Devon wound the recording forward and they listened again, and Naomi watched the brackets in her notebook with a strange unease. She had counted the exposition once. If it was played twice, then her careful grid had described a piece that didn't exist, a piece with half an opening. She had treated the form like a diagram to be filled in, and the diagram was true, but the music wasn't the diagram. The repetition wasn't redundancy; it was the piece putting its cards on the table twice so that the development's later betrayals, the minor keys, the fragments of the first theme pulled apart, would land on ears that already knew what was being broken.

"Your colours are wrong now," Devon said, not unkindly, tapping her notebook.

"They're not wrong. They're incomplete."

She started again with a pencil instead of the colours, and the second time through she didn't count, she just listened, and marked where the music seemed to leave the house it had built. It was near the double bar, just after the second theme settled in D. Whether the development truly began there or whether Mozart's transition blurred the line, she couldn't yet say, and Mr. Ferreira, when she asked him later that evening, only said, "Mark what you hear and be ready to defend it," which was less an answer than an invitation to be wrong in public.

Devon stayed while she worked, quieter than usual, and near the end of the hour he said that the repeat reminded him of his grandfather telling the same story at every dinner, the same words, until one night the words meant something different. Naomi didn't answer. She had her pencil at the recapitulation, where the opening theme came back in G, whole and unchanged, and she found she no longer trusted that unchangedness. It came back the same, but she was not the same listener, and whether that was what the form was for she couldn't prove. She underlined it lightly and wrote beside it, in small letters, maybe.

She played the movement once herself, badly, the chipped C clacking in the first theme. Devon turned the page for her at the repeat signs without being asked.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Mya taped the rehearsal schedule to the blackboard before anyone else arrived, then set nine pennies on the folding table like she'd watched the older counselor do at drama camp last summer. Heads were the actors who wanted the audience's attention, tails were the ones waiting for it. She slid a penny two inches and imagined Priya crossing downstage right, and for a moment the whole stage existed on a tabletop, small enough to control.

The one-act was hers. Ms. Rios had said it plainly, which was the problem: yours means you decide, and the deciding was what Mya had wanted until the moment she actually had to do it. Two weeks to opening, eight actors, a gym-turned-theater with a crepuscular light leak near the loading door that turned every evening scene the color of weak tea.

The trouble arrived at five after three, in the person of Devon, who played the brother and had been in three shows to Mya's zero. "I'm not doing that cross," he said, before she'd even finished placing him. "It's unnatural. Nobody walks away from an argument mid-line."

She had planned the scene on the table that morning, moving a dime where Devon now stood, and it had worked beautifully in miniature. Live, he loomed. The dime had never loomed at anything.

"It's called blocking," she said, which felt like saying something, though it wasn't. Later, when Priya asked why people even called it that, Mya told her what she'd learned at camp, from a counselor pushing coins around a picnic table: the word comes from nineteenth-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. Priya had looked at the pennies and said, "So we're all just blocks," and Mya had said, "Until you're people," and they'd both laughed, but she'd thought about it for days after.

Because that was the actual problem, she realized on the fourth day of Devon's resistance. A block cannot refuse a cross. It cannot tell you that a line lands better in stillness, and it cannot be right about that while you are wrong. Mya had been treating the directing like a kind of arbitrage, trading a small move here for a large effect there, certain the whole thing balanced if she just planned harder. Devon was doing something else: paying attention to one moment with everything he had.

She tried it his way. He stood planted through the argument, and the line went flat, and she said so, and he rolled his eyes but he heard her, she could tell, because at the next run-through he made the cross she'd asked for and then abandoned it halfway and found a third position neither of them had planned, by the window, half-turned, and suddenly the scene was better than her table and better than his stillness.

"Noted," she said, and wrote it down, and heard how stiff it sounded, so she added, "I'm not trying to exculpate my blocking by saying that. It's just better."

"I don't know what that means," Devon said.

"It means it's not my fault the blocking was wrong, but it's still my job to fix it." He almost smiled at that, which in Devon's currency was a substantial payment.

The light leak they couldn't fix; the custodian had tried twice. On the Friday before opening, Mya moved the final scene into the leak on purpose, let the actors drift into that gray-gold spill as the play wound down, and watched from the back row as the accident became a choice. Nothing about the week had gone to plan, and the coins sat untouched in her backpack, and she would use them again for the next show anyway, because a plan was a way of holding the stage in your hands before you had to open them. But she'd leave gaps between the pennies now. Room for a person to step off the table.

"Places," she called, and clapped twice, and eight actors turned toward her in the half-dark.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
The whiteboard had been Grandpa's, back when he sold insurance out of the spare room, and it still smelled faintly of dry-erase ink that had gone into the plastic years ago. Chase wheeled it out onto the screened porch after lunch, set his copy of Jane Eyre on the wicker table, and stood there for a while listening to the cicadas before he uncapped a marker. The assignment was due the first week of September, his first week of college, and the prompt had two boxes he was supposed to check: apply a feminist lens, or a Marxist one. He had circled both, then crossed out both, then circled both again.

He drew a line down the middle of the board. On the left he wrote OWNERS and on the right he wrote WORKERS, and underneath OWNERS he put Rochester, because a man with a house like Thornfield and tenants and land didn't work for anybody. Under WORKERS went Jane, then Mrs. Fairfax, then the housemaid Leah, then Bessie from Gateshead. He stepped back and looked at the columns. The whole novel sorted itself out that way in about four minutes, which felt too easy for something he was supposed to spend a summer thinking about.

His grandmother came out with two glasses of iced tea and set one down beside the book. She had been a school librarian for thirty years and had opinions about tea and about weather and, it turned out, about dry-erase markers, which she said were the worst thing ever invented for a porch because the dust got into everything. She read the board sideways, tilting her head.

"What's the rule for your two columns?" she asked.

"I'm working on it. In Marxist terms the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, like factories and land, and the proletariat owns only its labour and has to sell it for wages. So whoever has the land goes on the left."

"And Jane goes on the right because she sells her labour."

"Governessing is a job. She's basically an employee with a bedroom." He tapped the marker against his teeth. "But here's my problem. When she inherits from her uncle, she moves columns. Twenty thousand pounds, and suddenly she's on the left, and she only goes back to Rochester after she's rich. If the Marxist reading is right, the marriage at the end isn't romantic, it's a merger."

His grandmother settled into the rocking chair with the creak of old springs. "And the feminist reading?"

"The feminist reading says the inheritance matters because it's what makes her free to say yes. She won't marry him dependent. She says she's an independent woman now, right to his face." He wrote INHERITANCE with an arrow between the two columns. "But if that's true, then her freedom is just money, and the book can't imagine a woman being free without it. And if the Marxist reading is true, then the money just changes whose boot is on whose neck, except there's no boot at the end, there's just this quiet marriage in the woods. Both readings have to be a little wrong."

"Or both a little right," his grandmother said.

He wrote that at the bottom of the board anyway, because it was hers and he liked it. The afternoon light came through the screen in little diamonds on the floor. He tried drafting a thesis sentence aloud, something about how the novel expropriates Jane twice, first when her uncle's family takes her childhood and then when Rochester tries to take her story by making her a mistress instead of a wife, and his grandmother said she didn't think expropriate worked for the second one because nothing was being taken out of production, and he argued, and then he conceded, and the word came out of the draft.

The real problem he couldn't shake was smaller than the thesis. It was Bertha in the attic. She appeared in neither column. She didn't own anything, not even her own name in the text, and she didn't sell her labour either, so the entire system of sorting, the ontology of the board, had no box for her. He told his grandmother this, and she rocked for a while, and the ice shifted in her glass.

"Some people don't fit the categories," she said. "A good essay says so instead of pretending they do."

He wrote Bertha's name in the middle of the board, straddling the line, and looked at it. His thinking felt inchoate, all edges and no center, but that was closer to honest than either column was alone. He added a question mark next to her name and one next to the merger, and he took a photograph of the board with his phone before the porch light came on and washed the ink pale.

"What's for dinner?" he asked.

"Cold chicken," his grandmother said, standing, "and you're slicing the tomatoes."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
Isabelle had told herself, the night before, that she would walk through the gallery once, choose a wall, and start sketching, but the first thing she actually did was stand in the lobby and count the paintings she could see from the door. Twelve. The admissions counselor at the art school had said ten, unified by a single theme, accompanied by a statement of one page, and Isabelle had circled the word "unified" so many times in the brochure that the pen had torn through to the next page.

She found the Monet room by accident, or that was how she would describe it later, though in truth she had followed the crowd because the crowd looked like people who knew something. The walls held a run of cathedral facades, one after another, stone gone blue in some, blazing in others, and Isabelle stopped in front of a small placard that listed dates. She read it twice, and then a third time, mouthing the numbers. More than thirty views of the same facade, painted in 1892 and 1893. She turned and counted the canvases in the room, which was fewer than thirty, and felt briefly cheated, then less cheated, then something closer to stubbornness.

A woman with a lanyard was adjusting a rope barrier near the doorway. Isabelle asked her whether the paintings had all been done from the same spot. The woman said she believed so, that he had rented rooms across from the cathedral, that the light did the changing and he did the following. Then she moved on to a man photographing a fire exit, and Isabelle was left with the fact and her sketchbook.

Her own portfolio, at the moment, consisted of two paintings of the sugar maple in Mrs. Okafor's yard, one at dawn and one at dusk, and eight blank spaces in a list she had made on graph paper. She had been certain, a week ago, that this was too thin, that a committee would see the repetition as a failure of imagination, and she had begun planning instead a portfolio of ten different subjects: a portrait of her brother, a still life of the pharmacy counter where she worked Saturdays, the flooded quarry outside town. Ambition, her father called it. Desperation was closer, though she had not admitted that to anyone, and would not have admitted it even now, standing in front of the evidence against her plan.

She took out the sketchbook and drew the facade in the second painting, the one where the stone went rose and gold, working fast, not trying to copy but to catch what the light was doing to the surface. A tour group passed behind her. A boy about her age slowed, looked over her shoulder, and said, "You're drawing the painting instead of the wall." She said she was drawing the wall, Monet's wall, the one he had made out of light. The boy considered this, said "Huh," in a tone that could have meant anything, and drifted after the group.

Isabelle sat down on the bench in the center of the room. The light in here came from ceiling fixtures, obdurate and unchanging, nothing like the light on the canvases, which moved from canvas to canvas even though the paint itself had been dry for more than a century. She thought about the two maples. Dawn and dusk were the obvious pair, the postcard version, but the fact on the placard suggested something she had not considered: that the theme was not the tree at all. The theme was the watching. Monet had not painted thirty different cathedrals; he had painted one cathedral refusing to be the same twice. She flipped to a fresh page and wrote, in the corner where she could later preempt any committee's confusion by explaining it in the statement itself, "Same tree, ten hours, ten weathers." Then she crossed out "ten weathers," because she could not control the weather and did not want to promise what October might not deliver. She wrote "ten days" instead.

There was a deeper stratum to the problem, and she made herself look at it honestly rather than tucking it away. Ten paintings of one tree could still be a failure if she painted them lazily, if she leaned on Monet the way a student leans on a dictionary word, using the borrowed authority to excuse thin work. The thirty views were not impressive because they were thirty; they were impressive because each one had been fought for. She did not yet know whether she could fight like that. She knew the pharmacy counter would be easier, the portrait easier still, and easier was exactly the thing the counselor had warned about in the second paragraph of the handout, the paragraph Isabelle had skimmed.

She stayed until the attendant began walking the perimeter, glancing at her watch. On her way out Isabelle bought a postcard of the rose-and-gold facade, then stood at the lobby door with her sketchbook under her arm and the list of ten different subjects still folded in the back pocket of her jeans. She did not throw it away. It stayed there, a possibility, a hedge, through the bus ride home.

That evening she carried her portable easel to Mrs. Okafor's fence and set it up in the last flat light before sunset. The maple had lost three leaves since the dusk painting, and a fourth was letting go as she squeezed out her paints. She watched it twist all the way down and made a small mark on the canvas where it had been.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The marble slab had belonged to Edouard's mother, and it was the only thing in the kitchen he had never been allowed to touch. Now it sat on the counter in front of him, cold and gray as a headstone, while the chocolate in his bowl climbed toward forty-five degrees. He watched the thermometer the way other people watched hospital doors. His mother was three weeks gone, the funeral casseroles finally eaten, and Edouard had decided, without saying it aloud to anyone, that he would learn to temper chocolate before her birthday in June. She had made bars every winter, glossy things that broke with a sound like a knuckle cracking, and he had never once asked her how.

The first batch seized into a gritty paste while he looked away to answer a text. The second bloomed, as the forums called it, streaked white and dull, and when he broke a corner off it bent like an eraser before giving way. He poured both failures into a jar he was ashamed of and hid it behind the flour. His younger sister, Colette, drifted through the kitchen long enough to steal a piece of the failed batch and pronounce it "still chocolate," which was the kind of loyalty he could not decide whether he wanted.

He learned the vocabulary the way he learned anything now, alone at midnight: seed method, tabling, working temperature. He learned that real chocolate wanted a specific kind of attention, that you melted it hot, cooled it with chopped solid bits or against marble, and held it in a narrow window where it behaved. He was on his fourth attempt, spreading melted chocolate across the slab and scraping it back with the offset spatula, when his phone buzzed on the counter. It was Aurelio, voice-messaging from a campsite two counties over, where their class had gone for the long weekend.

"Dude, we made chocolate-dipped stuff on the fire," Aurelio's voice said over the hiss of the phone speaker. "My cousin brought these candy melts. We just melted them and dipped, and they hardened all shiny in like ten minutes. Nobody tempered anything. Is your whole marble slab thing a scam?"

Edouard set down the spatula. "What are candy melts exactly?"

"They're called compound chocolate, or coating chocolate," Aurelio said. "My cousin says the label says it. Anyway, they set without tempering. They come out glossy. But they don't have the same snap. Like, you bite it and it kind of gives."

Edouard looked at the chocolate cooling on the marble in front of him, at the ribbon of it lifting off the spatula, and felt something rearrange itself, not a conclusion exactly but the beginning of one. So there were two roads. One chocolate asked for everything, the melting and cooling, the temperature window, the marble, the patience, and gave back shine and a clean snap. Another replaced whatever made it demanding, and asked nothing, and set glossy anyway, and gave you something softer when you bit. Neither was a scam. They were different contracts. He texted back a single word, "no," and turned back to the slab before the chocolate overcooled.

The fourth attempt worked. He could tell before it set, because the chocolate on the marble stopped looking wet and began looking like something with intent, and when he pooled it back into the bowl and poured it into his mother's bar mold, it flowed like silk off a spoon. Twelve hours later he turned the mold over and the bars dropped out shining, and when he snapped one in half it made the sound, the exact sound, the knuckle crack, and Colette came running from the living room to see what it was.

They broke the bar between them on the back steps, and Edouard was already assembling a theory of what he had earned: that the failures were the price, that the marble mattered, that his mother's chocolate had cost her something every December and he had eaten it for seventeen years without paying his share. He was half through explaining this when Colette, who had gone quiet in a way he should have noticed, said, "You should look in the basement. The tall cabinet, behind the craft stuff."

He went down alone. In the cabinet, behind coils of ribbon and a box of ornaments, he found a half-empty bag of candy melts, orange and white discs gone slightly dusty, and beneath it his mother's bar mold, an older one, its cavities scarred from use, and a strip of masking tape across the bag in her handwriting that said only December. He stood there long enough for the basement light to click itself off, and then he stood there a while longer in the dark, holding the bag.

He did not tell Colette right away, partly because he did not know how, and partly because he understood, with a clarity that felt like cold water, that telling her would desensitize something in both of them, would sand down the memory of those winter bars into a smaller, truer, worse thing. His mother had taken a shortcut. She had used the coating chocolate that set without tempering, the kind that lacked the snap, and he had loved it anyway, had loved it specifically, the soft give of it against his teeth. Every glossy December bar of his childhood had been the easy kind, and his whole month of seized bowls and streaked failures had been spent chasing a sound he had never actually heard her make.

The next morning he was at the counter again, and Colette watched from the doorway, and neither of them said anything tangential or otherwise about the basement. He melted a handful of the candy melts in a bowl over warm water, plain, with no thermometer, no marble, no seeding, and dipped a strip of dried apricot in it the way Aurelio's cousin must have done by the fire. It set in the window sun in minutes, glossy and quick. He bit it. It gave, softly, without the snap, and it tasted almost, not quite, but almost like being ten years old in December.

He set a piece of it on the counter beside a shard of his tempered bar, the shining one that cracked like a knuckle, and pushed both toward his sister. Colette looked at them for a moment, then picked up the soft one, the one their mother would have made, and ate it without ceremony, watching him the whole time.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
Parker kept his thumb pressed against the edge of the page as though the article might slide off the desk. It was in Portuguese, four short paragraphs about a river festival in a town he had never heard of, and in twenty minutes he was supposed to stand and summarise it aloud. Ms. Ferreira, their regular teacher, was away on sabbatical, and the substitute had made it clear she would not be rescuing anyone. The classroom smelled of the wet coats drying by the radiator, and outside the window the creek that ran behind the gym had turned turbid after three days of rain, brown water moving fast under a grey sky. Parker read the first sentence again, then again, his lips moving over each word like a man counting coins.

Across the table, Dana was already on her third article. She turned pages the way other people shuffled cards. "You're reading every single word," she said, not looking up. "The substitute only asked for the date and the place. Just find them."

"That's cheating," Parker said. "She said summarise."

"She said summarise the article, and you can't summarise what you can't finish." Dana slid her chair around. "Here. Watch. When I read quickly for the general idea, that's skimming. When I'm hunting for one specific detail, like a name or a number, that's scanning. Different jobs." She ran her finger down the second paragraph without reading it, stopped, tapped twice. "There. The festival's on the fourteenth. You just spent ten minutes earning that."

Parker looked at the line she had tapped. The date sat there, plain as a coin in shallow water. He felt the small, ordinary humiliation of having done something the hard way and then seeing the easy way standing in plain sight. Still, he did not want to give up what he had gained. He had understood, word by slow word, that the festival had been held for sixty years, that the river mattered to the town, that the whole piece was quieter and sadder than a festival announcement had any right to be. Scanning would have missed that. He said so.

Dana had been confident a moment before, and now she was less so. She looked at her own three finished articles and wondered, for the first time that morning, what was actually in them. She had collected dates and names like a magpie and could not have said what any of the pieces were about. The substitute's voice drifted over from the window, telling someone that the exchange program that had brought Ms. Ferreira's class these newspapers was underwritten by a cultural foundation in Lisbon, and Dana thought about that word, underwritten, how something invisible held up the whole visible thing, how the general idea held up the details or maybe the details held up the general idea. She was not sure which. She turned back to her first article and began again, slowly this time.

Parker stood when his name was called. He kept his eyes off the page as much as he could, and what he gave was not elegant: a festival on a river, sixty years of it, a town that feared the river was changing. He mentioned the fourteenth. He mentioned the town's name, pronouncing it carefully, and heard the substitute say "good" in a way that meant she meant it. He sat down with his ears warm and watched Dana stand.

She summarised her first article well, better than she expected to, and Parker understood that she had gone back and read it properly after their argument, and that she would never say so. When the bell rang, the substitute collected the newspapers, and as she squared the stack she paused over Parker's page.

"This is a lovely piece," she said. "You know, it ran the year before last. The festival was cancelled after that. Floods." She nodded toward the window, toward the turbid creek rushing past the gym, and held out the stack. "Same river, different country."

Parker took his coat from the radiator and followed Dana out into the rain.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
Sienna sat on an upturned crate in the garage, the theory book open on her knees, while her father circled the car with a chamois leather as though it were a patient he did not trust the hospital to keep clean. Her practical test was at nine the next morning, and between her and that hour stood one small, specific fear. In six months of lessons she had rehearsed bay parking until she could do it in her sleep, reversing neatly between the white lines of the supermarket, but she had never once pulled up beside a kerb and backed in. Her instructor had said it might not come up. Might, she kept thinking, was a word doing a lot of heavy lifting.

"Say something else that might not come up," she said. "Exams. Weather. Life."

Her father stopped polishing. "My test, years ago, the examiner asked me to do the parallel park. I clipped the kerb and failed." He said it lightly, the way people mention things they have spent decades quietly trying to expiate. "So I've always had a soft spot for that manoeuvre. Terrible reason to teach it to you, I suppose."

She looked up from the book. "Wait. They can just ask for it?"

"Parallel parking's one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask you to do," he said, as if reciting something learned by heart and half forgotten. "At the side of the road. They choose."
