She stared at him. Six months of bay parking, of positioning between painted lines as tame as graph paper, and the whole time there had been this other door. "Why didn't anyone say?"

"Your instructor likes bays. Bays are clean." He shrugged, which she recognised as his way of admitting the fault was shared. It was, in its way, a very cerebral evasion, all reasoning and no responsibility, and she filed it away to argue with later. Not tonight. Tonight there was a kerb.

The garage opened onto the cul-de-sac, and the cul-de-sac had a stretch of pavement with two wheelie bins standing in for the cars she would have to slot between. Her father dragged the bins out himself, wanting to be useful, wanting, she suspected, to put his own failed test to rest by proxy, to watch a version of himself succeed. That was his want, and she decided she could lend herself to it. She pulled up alongside the first bin, checked her mirrors the way the book insisted, and began to reverse.

She was bad at it. Three times the rear wheel kissed the kerb with a sound like a knuckle cracking, and each time she pulled forward and started again, wondering why the wheel didn't simply follow her intention. On the fourth attempt she stopped halfway through and sat with her hands on the wheel, thinking about the bins, the kerb, the arc the car wanted to make whether she asked for it or not. The bay park had been maths; this was closer to a negotiation. "It's not that I steer it," she said slowly. "It's that it turns and I ask permission."

Her father leaned in the doorway, not correcting her, which was new. "Want to try the road by the shops? There's a proper kerb."

The road by the shops led to the ring road, and the ring road led to the slip road, and somewhere in that chain of decisions she found herself accelerating down a ramp with traffic behind her, her father saying nothing at all, which was either trust or terror. She matched her speed to the gap in the near lane, glanced, signalled, slid in. The car behind never braked. Something in her chest unlocked. Merging, she decided, was the parallel park turned inside out, the same question asked at forty miles an hour: how do you join a system that was already moving?

They came home in the dark and she parallel parked between the bins one last time, clean, wheels close to the kerb, and sat with the engine ticking. She still did not know what tomorrow's examiner would ask for. Maybe a bay, maybe the road. Maybe the whole distinction between practised and unpractised was thinner than she had believed, and confidence was only fear that had found a gap and slipped into it. Her father knocked on the window and held up two fingers, meaning attempts remaining before her aunt arrived to take the car to the garage for its service, meaning their deadline had shrunk, meaning practice was over whether she was finished or not.

"Once more," Sienna said, and pulled forward to the start of the kerb.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The essay was due at eight the next morning, and Jaxon had written nothing but his name. He sat at the kitchen table with Pride and Prejudice open to the passage Ms. Okafor had assigned, the one where Charlotte Lucas accepts Mr. Collins, and beside it his notes from the unit on critical lenses, two columns headed FEMINIST and MARXIST that had so far received only a single question mark each. His mother was steaming broccoli at the stove, and his grandmother, who had arrived that afternoon with a suitcase and a lemon cake, was cutting the cake into slices nobody had asked for and everybody would eat.

"Charlotte is twenty-seven," Jaxon said, mostly to himself. "She says she's a burden on her parents. She marries the most annoying man in England on purpose."

His grandmother set a plate in front of him, cake first, homework second, which told him exactly where his evening ranked in her cosmology. "In my day," she said, "we called a girl like that sensible, and people called her worse. Sensible or a burden, depending on who was talking."

"That's the thing, though. Who's talking?" He pushed the plate an inch away, then pulled it back. "If I use the feminist lens, Charlotte's choice isn't really hers. She was trained to want security because that's all they let women want. If I use the Marxist lens, it's about money, her class, the fact that she has no property and Mr. Collins has a house. But those overlap so much I can't tell them apart, and Ms. Okafor wants us to bring them together, not just stack them."

His mother turned down the burner and sat across from him, still holding the wooden spoon. "There's a book on the shelf behind you," she said. "Your aunt left it when she moved. The thick one with the cracked spine. She quoted it at every holiday for about four years."

He found it wedged between cookbooks: The Second Sex, Simone de Beauvoir, the translation dated 1949 on the copyright page. He'd expected a screed, something that malign men as a class, and instead the pages were dense and careful, argument built on argument. His aunt had underlined one sentence in pencil so many times the paper had gone soft: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.

"One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman," he read aloud.

His grandmother stopped with the knife halfway through the cake. "That's true," she said, in a different voice than before, quieter. "Nobody hands you a list, but you get trained all the same. How to sit. What to want. What to be grateful for." She looked at the knife, then finished the cut and laid the slice down gently. "Your great-aunt wanted to be a surveyor. She became a wife instead, and she was good at it, and everyone said she was lucky, including her, I think, out loud, at every dinner for fifty years."

Jaxon wrote the line on his notecard, then the publication year, then stopped. "So Beauvoir would say Charlotte's wanting the house is trained into her. Society makes the womanhood before Charlotte ever gets to choose. But then the money part still matters, because the training only works because women can't own anything." He looked up. "So the lenses aren't two separate tools. The economic trap is part of how the training happens. Charlotte's choice is real and it's conditioned at the same time, and she knows it, that's the worst part, she literally says she's not romantic."

"So which is it," his mother said, "her choice or her training?"

"That's what I can't decide. And I don't think Beauvoir decides it either." He turned the notecard over. "Maybe that's the position. That it's both, and the essay is about how you can't pull them apart." Even as he said it, he heard Ms. Okafor's voice in his head asking whether that was an answer or an excuse for not having one, and he honestly did not know. He ate a bite of cake to keep from writing that down.

His grandmother carried a slice to his mother without being asked, because his mother never took one for herself, and came back drying her hands on the dish towel. "Write your both," she said. "If you turn in only one, you'll be wrong in a way you can't defend. If you turn in both and say you're stuck, at least you're stuck in the right place."

He pulled the laptop toward him and typed the first real sentence of the essay, then deleted half of it, then typed it again with the quotation worked in, one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, and after it the words Though Charlotte Lucas speaks as if her pragmatism were a private peccadillo, Beauvoir suggests the wish itself was assembled for her, and outside the window the streetlight came on, which meant it was past nine, which meant he had three hours.

"Grandma," he said, "why did Aunt Denise stop quoting this book?"

His grandmother considered the cake, the stove, the boy at the table with his deadline. "She didn't stop," she said. "She just started quoting it to her students instead of to us. She teaches now, in the city, the whole cosmopolitan thing. Fill your thermos, you're going to be up late."

He got up and filled the thermos.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
Grandmother's kitchen smelled of scorched butter and old newsprint, and Justine sat at the table with her phone face-down like a suspect being interrogated. On the screen was the draft of a message she had written and deleted four times since Tuesday, each version worse than the last. The current draft read, in its entirety, "hey, about the presentation." Period. Full stop. Coward's punctuation.

"Who died?" Grandmother asked, setting down a plate of scones that had clearly lost an argument with the oven.

"Nobody. It's Priya. She was supposed to send her slides two days before our demo and she sent them at midnight, so I redesigned half of them at one in the morning and then in class she told Mr. Okafor the visuals were a team effort." Justine heard her own voice climb and cut it short.

"So you're going to send her something charming like 'you ruined it.'"

"I was considering it."

Grandmother slid a book across the table, a paperback with a cracked spine, the kind of thing she kept around the way other grandmothers kept hard candy. "Your grandfather's. From when he was teaching. There's a chapter in there that saved more faculty meetings than the coffee budget ever did." She went back to the stove, which was her way of leaving the room without leaving it.

Justine opened the book. It was about conflict, and about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, who back in the 1960s had promoted something the book called I-messages: saying "I felt stuck when the slides came in late" instead of pointing a finger and saying "you ruined it." The idea was to raise a problem without blaming. She read the page twice, then turned her phone over and started typing, out loud, because the kitchen was empty enough to allow it.

"You made everything late and then you took credit." She stopped. Tried again. "The slides came in late and I felt stuck." Better, but it still sounded like a hostage statement. "Priya, when the slides came in at midnight, I felt stuck, because I rebuilt half the deck on no sleep, and in class I didn't know how to say that without making it sound like an accusation, which maybe this still does, but I'm sending it anyway." She looked up. Grandmother was watching from the counter with an expression of profound, scone-related innocence.

"You're eavesdropping."

"I'm supervising. There's a difference. It's the difference between a lifeguard and a gossip." Grandmother came and sat down, breaking a scone in half without eating either part. "In my day we had a girl like this on my netball team. Beautiful passer, couldn't take a note. We all just stopped telling her anything and she never got better and none of us liked her and she never knew why. Impermeable, that girl. Nothing got through, because we never tried to get anything through."

"That's depressing."

"That's the alternative, yes." Grandmother stood and dusted crumbs off her apron. "You could also consider that Priya might have a reason. Her mother was in the hospital, I hear, from your mother, who hears everything, which is a separate condition we don't need to treat today."

Justine sat with that. It reframed things without dissolving them; Priya's midnight might have been a bad midnight too, and it changed nothing about the one o'clock redesign, the two o'clock alarm, the five o'clock walk to school in the dark feeling like the whole group project had ionized into separate charges, all of them repelling each other. A reason and a problem could occupy the same person. She had been treating them like they couldn't.

She typed a new version. "Priya, I heard about your mom and I hope she's okay. Separately, and I'm still saying it because it mattered: when the slides came in the night before, I felt stuck, and I ended up redoing a lot on no sleep, and then when it got called a team effort I didn't know what to do with that. Can we set an earlier cutoff for the next one? Like, real deadlines, not decorative ones." She read it aloud, quietly, testing it against Gordon's old formula. It raised the problem. It did not blame. It also did not pretend the problem hadn't happened, which she suspected was where the whole method went soft if you let it.

"You've read it nine times," Grandmother said. "Aesthetes rewrite. Cowards reread."

"I'm being careful."

"You're stalling." Grandmother picked up the phone, held it just out of reach, which at seventy-four she could still do to a girl who let her, and raised an eyebrow with the full authority of someone who had once made a headmistress cry. "Careful is when you check the recipient. Stalling is when you check it nine times. Send it, or I will compose a message myself, in cursive, and mail it to her house, where her recovering mother will have to carry it upstairs."

"You wouldn't."

"I have stationary and I have stamps and I have absolutely nothing else to do this afternoon."

Justine took the phone back, put her thumb over the send button, and breathed out through her nose, one long controlled exhale like they taught in choir before a solo. Somewhere between the butter smell and the ruined scones and the cracked paperback she had stopped being sure whether she was doing this for the project, for Priya, or for the version of herself who didn't want to become the netball team. She pressed send before she could rank them.

The checkmark turned blue. Then three dots appeared, the small patient kind that could mean anything, and Grandmother said, "Now eat a scone, it'll put hair on your chest, which is not what we want either," and the phone buzzed in Justine's hand.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The Portuguese booth at the harvest festival had a folding table, a stack of newspapers, and a sign that read "Read the News With Us," which Henry had walked past twice before stopping. He needed the language for a college placement test in the fall, and more than that, he needed proof to himself that a summer of flashcards had turned into something he could actually use. The woman at the table handed him a short article from a Lisbon daily and asked him to summarize it aloud when he was ready. She would listen, she said, and correct nothing unless he asked.

He sat on the grass behind the booth with the article and a pencil, and he began the way he always began, with the first sentence, working word by word like a man laying bricks. The first sentence gave him trouble. It mentioned a court, a river, a company, and a subpoena, and the grammar kept rearranging itself whenever he thought he had it pinned. He lost ten minutes there, sweating over whether the river belonged to the company or the company to the river, before moving on. The second sentence was easier, and the third easier still, but by the time he reached the final paragraph he felt he had only fragments, and so he did what seemed sensible: he started decoding the last paragraph first, reasoning that endings must be conclusions, and conclusions must hold the point.

The last paragraph was about a woman who owned a bakery near the courthouse. She had opinions about parking. He read it four times, wrote out a translation, and understood it completely, and it told him nothing about anything. A guy around his age, wearing a volunteer shirt from the festival, wandered over and looked at the paper upside down in Henry's hands. "You're doing the end first," the guy said. It wasn't a question.

"Endings are the point," Henry said, feeling defensive about a method he had never actually examined.

The guy crouched and tapped the opening paragraph. "News is written the other way. It's called the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the less important details follow." He said it lightly, the way you'd tell someone the bathroom was around the back, and then he stood up and drifted toward the food stalls without checking whether Henry believed him.

Henry sat with that for a moment, because it was a strange idea, and he tested it against what he knew. He thought about English news he'd read his whole life, and yes, the who and what were always in the first line, and the bakery lady, the human detail, the texture, always came last. So the paragraph he had wrestled for ten minutes, the one with the subpoena, that was the core of the story, and he had treated it as an obstacle on the way to the real part. He went back to it with new eyes. Knowing that the essential facts were all in that opening, he stopped trying to extract every grammatical filament and instead asked what the sentences had to assert. A court had ordered a company to hand over documents. The company had dumped something in the river. He couldn't tell what exactly, and he couldn't tell when, and he wasn't sure he cared, or whether not caring was laziness or reasonable triage.

He wondered, too, whether the pyramid shape did something to the reader beyond saving time. If the important stuff came first, then the article assumed you might leave at any moment, assumed your attention was a resource it had to win immediately. That felt almost rude, and also honest. His English teacher had denigrated news writing all spring as shallow compared to literature, and Henry had accepted it, but sitting here he wasn't sure shallow was the word. The bakery paragraph was the part that made the story human, and the pyramid said it was the least important part. Both things seemed true at once, and he didn't know yet how to hold them together.

He walked back to the table. The woman set down her cup of coffee and waited, and a small half-circle of festival-goers had gathered, including the guy in the volunteer shirt, who gave Henry a nod that could have meant anything. Henry spoke his summary aloud, his accent cerebral and careful where it should have been quick: a company had polluted a river, a court had issued a subpoena for its documents, and the story mattered because of what came in the opening paragraph. The woman smiled at that last part. He added, honestly, that he didn't know the dates or the fine amounts, and that the ending, about the woman and the parking, was the part he'd understood best and the part he'd understood least.

"Say the last part again," the woman said. "About the bakery."

He did, and the guy in the volunteer shirt laughed, quietly, like someone who had read the whole article already and knew exactly why.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
The kitchen smelled of coffee and the Sunday paper, both of them Grandfather's habits, and neither of them had stopped just because Grandfather was in Ward Four of the Royal Infirmary. Ethan sat at the table with the Portuguese weekly folded open in front of him, the way Grandfather had left it a week ago, creased to page seven, where a short article about a flood in a northern province waited to be read. For eleven years, Sunday mornings had meant Grandfather reading one article aloud in Portuguese and then summarizing it for Ethan in English, a slow ceremony that Ethan had endured more than enjoyed. Now the paper had come through the letterbox without its reader, and Grandmother had set it at Ethan's place before he came downstairs, saying nothing.

He had wanted, for a long time, to be the one doing the reading instead of receiving it. Grandfather had offered to teach him properly, year after year, and year after year Ethan had put it off with the ease of someone who assumed there would always be another summer. What he had instead was a half vocabulary, a tourist's accent, and a promise made at the hospital window on Thursday, when Grandfather, with the stoicism that made even his illnesses seem like a posture he had chosen, said, "Sunday. Page seven. Don't skip it." Ethan had said he wouldn't, and had not dared, then or since, to impute any larger meaning to the request, though the word promise kept attaching itself to it anyway.

The article was four paragraphs. He could identify that much. He could identify "inundações" because Grandfather had once spent a whole breakfast on words for water, and he could find the province on the map in his phone, but between those two footholds the sentences kept collapsing under him, verbs changing shape in ways nobody had ever warned him about. Grandmother moved around the kitchen, drying cups that were already dry, and he could feel her listening to his silences the way you feel rain starting on a roof.

"Try the first line," she said. "Loud. He always said the mouth learns before the eye."

He read it aloud, and it came out half-decent, and she nodded as though it had come out perfect, which somehow made it worse. Then she drifted to the counter, where her own paper lay, the English one, opened to a headline she had been circling with her finger all morning. "Tell me this, then," she said. "Since you're the scholar today. 'Council Rejects Housing Plan.' Where is the rest of it? Where is the the? And why rejects, when this happened Tuesday? The paper knows it already happened."

Ethan looked at the headline and, for a moment, felt the ground tilt in the useful way it did in exams, when a wrong-looking thing suddenly revealed its own logic. The words weren't broken. They were compressed. "They leave the small words out," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "The, a, is. And they use the present for things that already happened. Rejects, not rejected." She frowned at the page as if it had been rudely clipped. "Grandpa called that once," she said. "He called it headlinese. When he worked at the print shop, the men joked in headlinese. 'Ethan Misses Bus.' That kind of thing."

He laughed, and the laugh loosened something, and he looked back at the Portuguese page and found that the headline there was short too, and that some part of his fear of it had been a fear of newspaper language itself, its appetite for cutting whatever could be cut. He would not claim the two languages did the same thing; he only knew that reading like a reader of papers, expecting the fewest words doing the most work, made the page less hostile. He worked through the first paragraph aloud, stopped, asked Grandmother for "inundar," which she gave him without pausing, and did not ask why a woman who dried clean cups had flood vocabulary ready.

The second paragraph contained the name of a village, and he was two sentences into it before he noticed that Grandmother had gone still at the sink. "That's where he was born," she said. "Not that village, the next one. The river comes down between them." The article, he realized, was not about a place he didn't know. It was about a place that had sent his grandfather out at nineteen with one suitcase, and the coincidence felt less like coincidence the longer he sat with it, though he could not have said what it felt like instead.

He summarized it for her in English, the way Grandfather used to, and his summary was clumsy and honest: heavy rain, a river over its banks, an old stone bridge closed, farmers moving livestock, an official quoted saying the bridge would be assessed. It was a small story about a small place, and he delivered it in the flat voice of a summary, and Grandmother sat down across from him and listened to all of it.

Then she told him the thing he had not thought to wonder about. "You know I never understood his readings," she said. "Forty years of Sundays. Portuguese went in one ear and out the other, and after, over lunch, he'd tell me in English what it said, but that wasn't the point, love. The point was his voice in the house on a Sunday, going on about floods and elections in a village I've never seen. I could have had the news off the television any day of the week." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I thought it would be a comfort, you reading it. And it is, and it isn't, because it means he's not here to do it, and because you sound a little like him when you get going."

Ethan had come downstairs believing the task was the translation, the grammar, the getting through page seven, and he understood now that he had been solving the smaller problem. He could not give her Grandfather's voice, and he said so, and she said, "No, but you'll get better, and I'll get used to it, and that's how it goes." She folded Grandfather's paper and put it on the shelf where the previous eleven years of them stood in a neat brown stack, then changed her mind and took it back down and set it in front of him again. "Page eleven next week," she said. "There's an article about the wine harvest, and he'd have wanted it read properly."

He would have to work for that one too, verbs he didn't know and words for vines, and probably he would get half of it wrong and she would nod anyway. He slid the paper toward himself, creased page eleven the way Grandfather's hands used to, and said, "Tell him Thursday I've got homework for him when he's home."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
The grocery store parking lot at nine on a Sunday morning was half empty, which was exactly why Madison's mother had chosen it. Two abandoned shopping carts stood near the cart corral, maybe eight feet apart, and her mother parked the car, got out, and positioned them like cones. "You are not," she said through the window, "to impugn my cart placement. I measured with my feet."

"You measured with your feet," Madison said.

"A foot is a foot."

She pulled forward until the cart on the left sat even with her hip, reversed with the wheel cut hard right, then straightened, then cut left, and eased back into the imaginary space. She clipped the rear cart with her bumper, not hard, and both of them watched it roll away toward a paper recycling bin as though it had somewhere to be.

"Okay," Madison said. "That cart was being pugnacious."

"That cart was stationary. You hit a stationary cart."

"That's worse, actually." She laughed despite herself, and her mother got out again to retrieve it, walking with the unhurried patience of a woman who had done this before, with an older cousin, years ago, on a lot behind a church. The second attempt was better. The third was nearly clean, the tires a decent distance from the curb of the cart corral, and by the sixth she could do it without narrating to herself, which she considered real progress, since narrating had felt like a crutch.

The problem was that parallel parking was the small, polite part of the test, and the highway was the other one. On the way home they would merge onto Route 9, and merging was a thing Madison had been avoiding in her mind the way you avoid thinking about a dentist appointment two weeks out. Her mirrors seemed honest. She adjusted them in the lot, angled out so she could see the edge of the lot and a man in a green apron collecting carts near the entrance, wheeling them in a long rattling train behind him.

The drive started calm. Then came the ramp, the short one, the one her mother called "the launch," and Madison accelerated with the traffic, signaled, and glanced at the side mirror, which showed empty road. She began to drift left.

"Shoulder," her mother said, quiet but fast.

Madison looked over her right shoulder and there was a car, a gray sedan, close enough that she could see the driver's sunglasses, sitting in a place the mirror had never mentioned. She eased back into her lane, hands steady only because she made them be, and the sedan passed on without honking, which felt like a small mercy.

"Blind spot," Madison said a minute later, when her breathing had evened out. "The mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind the car."

"That's why the shoulder check," her mother said. "Before you merge, before you change lanes. Every time, even when the mirror looks empty." She didn't lecture beyond that; she just pointed at the next lane change three exits later and let Madison do it herself, mirror first, then chin over the shoulder, then the move, smooth and legal. The gray sedan was gone. Somewhere behind them, a man in a green apron was still collecting carts, and the two carts she'd borrowed were back in the corral, and the whole world of the parking lot had closed behind her like water.

What Madison turned over, on the straight stretch before their exit, was not fear but a kind of arithmetic. Her instructor at school had said trust your mirrors, keep your eyes forward, scan every few seconds, and there was truth in that; you couldn't drive with your head swiveling like a owl's. But the mirrors lied by omission, quietly, in a band of space right beside her where a whole car could hide. So the answer wasn't mirrors or shoulder checks, it was both, in a rhythm: mirror for the wide picture, shoulder for the gap the mirror couldn't hold. What she still didn't know was the exact timing, how fast a glance could be before it stopped being a glance, and she decided she'd have to find that out by doing it, badly at first, probably with her mother's hands tightening on the door handle in silent complicity.

"There's a cart at home in the driveway, by the way," her mother said as they took the exit. "From Tuesday. If you can parallel park between it and the mailbox, I'll make pancakes."

"You stole a cart?"

"Borrowed. It's a complicity situation. You were in the car."

Madison slowed at the light and looked both ways, an ordinary intersection, no trick to it at all, and yet she checked twice. At home she backed between the cart and the mailbox in one clean motion, killed the engine, and sat there a second, looking at the cart like a defeated opponent.

"Where do we return it?" she said.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
The writing club met on Thursdays in the library's conference room, a glass box near the biographies, and Mia arrived early enough to claim the chair by the window. Outside, October was doing something lugubrious with the sky, all low gray cloud and slow rain, and she watched a groundskeeper drag a tarp across the tennis courts while she waited for the others. She had her history paper in her bag, folded once even though that was bad for paper, like the paper was contraband.

"You brought it," Dev said, dropping into the seat across from her. "The one Mr. Halvorsen wrote all over."

"He wrote one thing all over it." She unfolded the pages on the table. At the bottom of the last page, where Mia had listed her sources under the heading she'd used all through freshman and sophomore English, Halvorsen had circled it twice and written, "See me," in red ink that looked angrier than the words. Six sources. The Dust Bowl, Dorothea Lange, an argument about photography and federal policy. She'd worked on it for two weeks.

Priya leaned over from the next chair, reading upside down. "What's wrong with it? Those look like real sources."

"That's what I said." Mia turned the paper right side up for her. "I cited everything. Lange's own caption, the historian from the journal, all of it. In the text I put the names and the page numbers in parentheses, like you're supposed to. And then at the end..."

"Works Cited," Priya read aloud.

Dev winced. "In a history class? Halvorsen wants a bibliography. My sister had him. He's obsessive about it. You keep the citations inside the paper the same way, the name and page number, but at the end he wants it called a bibliography, and he wants it to look right."

"That's it? The whole thing is one word?" Mia heard how loud she'd gotten and lowered her voice. "He circled one word and wrote 'see me' like I'd plagiarized something."

"He wouldn't impugn your whole paper over a heading," Priya said. "He wrote 'strong claim' next to your thesis. In red, but still."

Mia looked at the thesis. She had argued that Lange's photographs did not simply document the migrants' suffering but pressured the federal government to act, and one of her sources, a historian named Whitfield, had argued almost the opposite, that the photographs came after the policies and prettified their etiology, turning structural failure into weather and dust and faces. Mia had put both sources in the paper. She hadn't decided yet whether she believed one of them or something between them, and she'd been half hoping Halvorsen wouldn't notice the gap. He'd noticed. "Muddles two views; which is yours?" he'd written on page three.

The club advisor, Ms. Okonkwo, came in with a thermos and a stack of returned short stories, and the meeting officially began, but the conference table was small and the conversation didn't stay on the stories for long. Dev told the whole group about the heading. Tomas, a senior, laughed into his sleeve.

"That's not even the worst Halvorsen story," Tomas said. "He once made a kid redo a paper because the kid called it a 'reference page.' But here's the thing. He's right that it matters. Not the word itself. The discipline of it. In English class you learned one convention and it became invisible to you. It's like an accent. You don't hear your own."

"Then I have an English accent," Mia said.

"You have an English accent," Tomas agreed, "and it took you two years to find out."

She laughed, but later, when the others were workshopping Priya's story about a lighthouse keeper, Mia read her own paper again under the table. The heading had been invisible, sure. But so had the other thing, the muddle, and she didn't think that one was about convention. She took out a pen and, in the margin beside Whitfield, wrote "but Lange photographed BEFORE the policy changed, check dates," and then sat looking at that, because she wasn't sure the dates settled it either. Two ways of seeing the same photographs, and her paper had let them stand side by side like guests at a party who hadn't been introduced.

After the meeting she stayed behind while Ms. Okonkwo stacked chairs. "Can I ask you something that isn't about the club?"

"You just did."

"If I rewrite the ending and I still don't know which side I'm on. Is that a bad paper?"

Ms. Okonkwo considered the question the way she considered everything, without hurrying. "It depends on whether you've earned the not-knowing. A paper that hides indecision is bad. A paper that has done the work and lands somewhere honest, even if it's somewhere unfinished, is usually the better one."

Mia nodded and put the pages back in her bag, unfolded this time. On Monday she would go in during Halvorsen's free period. She'd change the heading, obviously, that was five minutes, and then she'd tell him about the dates she'd checked, and the part she still couldn't settle, and see what he said. In the parking lot the rain had stopped and the tarp on the tennis courts had collected a shallow pool of water at its center, bright against the gray, like something photographed on purpose.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezing food at -18 degrees Celsius (0 degrees Fahrenheit) stops bacteria from growing but does not kill most of them, so thawed food can spoil again.
story:
Devin's kitchen smelled like onions and printer ink, because the meal plan was still coming out of the printer while the first pan was already heating. Joshua stood at the counter with the pages warm in his hand, seven dinners laid out in a grid, and tried to believe that this was a thing he could actually do. His mother had cooked every meal of his life until June. In three weeks he would be in a dorm with a shared kitchenette and a meal plan that ran out, apparently, sometime around Thursday of every week, and he had asked Devin, of all people, to teach him how to survive.

"First thing," Devin said, tapping the grid, "is that you cook for Sunday and Thursday at the same time. Two chickens, one oven, four containers each." Devin was pre-med and treated groceries like a lab protocol, which was either reassuring or alarming. Joshua had come thinking he would learn recipes. He was beginning to understand he was learning logistics.

They made a list on the back of a receipt, drove to the store with the windows down, and argued in the produce section about whether a bag of carrots that costs less per pound but spoils faster is actually cheaper. Joshua held both bags and turned them over like a judge weighing evidence. "It depends on whether I eat them," he said finally, and Devin laughed and said that was true of almost everything, which struck Joshua as both obvious and somehow profound, the kind of thing he would have rolled his eyes at a year ago.

Back at the house, the work was real and unglamorous. They salted the chickens, portioned ground turkey into five plastic bags, and labeled everything with a marker that was running dry. Joshua kept forgetting to wash his hands between the raw chicken and everything else, and Devin kept catching him without making a speech about it, just pointing at the sink. By the time the oven was preheated, the counter looked like a functioning kitchen, which surprised Joshua, since it had looked like chaos the entire time it was becoming one.

Then came the problem. Devin's freezer was small and already half full of his roommate's mystery boxes, and when they tried to fit the turkey in, the shelf buckled and one bag slid loose, its zip seal split, raw meat smeared across the ice tray. They cleaned it, re-bagged it, and reorganized, and Joshua discovered that a freezer has a kind of geography, that things get lost in it the way socks get lost in a dormer. One container of cooked chicken from last month turned up at the back, frost-furred, unlabeled, and Joshua pulled it out and set it on the counter while they worked.

"You're not going to eat that," Devin said, without looking up from the stove.

"It's frozen," Joshua said. "Frozen things are fine, right? Nothing grows in there. It's like pausing them."

Devin turned around then, and instead of lecturing, asked it like a quiz question, which Joshua suspected was worse. "What temperature does my freezer run at?" Joshua read the little dial. Negative eighteen Celsius. "Okay, and what does that actually do?"

Joshua stood there holding the frosty container and worked through it out loud, slowly, the way he did with calculus. "It stops bacteria from growing," he said. "But it doesn't kill them. It's not sterilizing anything. It's more like..." He searched for it. "Like they're all just waiting."

"So what happens when it thaws?"

"They wake up. They go back to normal. So thawed food can spoil again, same as fresh." He looked at the container in his hand and then at the counter where it had sat for twenty minutes, sweating. "So this isn't safe just because it was frozen. It's only as safe as however long it's been warm."

"Was that a guess or do you actually know it?" Devin asked, and Joshua had to admit it was reasoning, not knowledge, and Devin said that reasoning plus a thermometer was how people stayed alive in labs. They threw the old container out. Joshua felt a small, specific vertigo, the kind he got when a thing he'd assumed was a wall turned out to be a window. All those years of frozen leftovers at home, and he had never once wondered what the cold was doing, only that it worked.

They ate the first meal at the little table by the window, chicken and rice and the carrots they'd debated, and Joshua kept the meal plan pages next to his plate, annotating them. He wrote thaw in fridge, never on counter next to Thursday, then crossed it out and wrote it bigger. He caught himself lecturing himself in the margins, his mother's voice creeping in through his own handwriting, and he excoriated himself silently for it, then softened, because honestly it wasn't the worst voice to have along.

They argued companionably about how much of this was actually about food. Joshua said he thought the whole afternoon was secretly about time, about knowing where a thing was in its life, frozen or fresh or on its way to spoiling. Devin said that was the most germane thing Joshua had said all day, second only to the carrot insight, and Joshua threw a balled-up napkin at him. Devin ducked and said that if Joshua wanted to keep pontificating he could at least learn to pronounce "braise," since he'd been saying "bray-zee" like it had some extra syllable, and for the next five minutes they abandoned food safety entirely for phonetics, sounding the word out together over the plates like two kids reading aloud.

It was dark when Joshua carried his four containers to the car. The cooked chicken went into the cooler he'd brought, the raw turkey stayed frozen in Devin's freezer to be picked up tomorrow, and on the drive home he kept glancing at the cooler on the passenger seat, wondering how long it would stay cold, whether he should stop and get ice, what his mother would say about any of it. At the next red light he picked up his phone and typed a reminder into it, then sat there after the light turned green, holding the screen, reading the words thaw in fridge over and over until the car behind him honked.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
Daniel pushed his potatoes to the edge of his plate and waited for his mother to finish telling his aunt about the neighbor's fence. It was Sunday dinner, which meant everyone stayed at the table until the dishes went cold, which meant there was time, if he could find a way in.

"Marcus read my history essay," he said, into a gap in the conversation. "The one for the team submission."

His father looked up. "The boy who got into Georgetown?"

"He tore it apart. Three pages of comments." Daniel kept his voice flat. "Half of them just say 'unclear' or 'weak.' One of them says 'awkward,' next to a sentence I worked on for an hour."

"Sounds like he did you a favor," his father said.

"Sounds like he did himself a favor." Daniel heard his own sharpness and pulled it back. "He gets to look like the smart one, and I get to figure out what 'awkward' means. I'm not revising anything tonight. If I even open that document again it'll be to delete it."

His aunt set down her fork. "So what will you do?"

"Nothing. He's my teammate. We present together on Thursday." He cut a potato in half without eating it. "I have to say something to him about how he gives feedback, because if he does that to Priya before the next draft, she'll shut down completely. She already thinks the whole team sees her as the weak one. A comment like 'weak' on her section is a disincentive to ever showing anyone a draft again."

"So tell him he's rude," his father said.

"That's not feedback either. That's just a smaller version of the same thing. A label instead of a note." Daniel knew he was talking partly to himself now, and let it happen, because the table was quiet and listening. "Mrs. Okafor does something different. When she hands back essays she writes all over them, worse than Marcus, honestly, but at the top of mine last month she wrote, 'I'm pushing you because I know you can write better than this.' And I rewrote the whole thing that night. Marcus's three pages just made me want to quit."

His mother tilted her head. "That's just her being nice."

"It's not nice. Her comments were harder than his." He turned his fork over. "I looked it up, actually, because it seemed strange. In 2014 there was a study led by a researcher named David Yeager. Students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. Not softer comments. The same comments, plus one sentence of belief."

"So you're saying Marcus should lie to you," his father said.

"Marcus thinks I'm lazy. That's the actual problem. His comments aren't the worst part. The worst part is that they all come with this... assumption underneath, that I'm not trying." Daniel stopped, made himself introspect for a second instead of escalating, and realized his father had a point buried in the provocation. "No. He doesn't have to lie. He has to say what he actually believes, if he believes anything, and if he doesn't, then I'd rather know that too."

The food was getting cold and nobody seemed to care. His aunt asked what he would say to Marcus tomorrow, and Daniel said he didn't know yet, and his sister snorted, and he let that pass.

He drafted it on the bus, in the margin of his chemistry notes, crossing out anything that sounded like a verdict. "Your comments on my essay" became "when you wrote 'awkward' on page two." "You're harsh" became "I couldn't tell what to change." By third period he had three sentences, and by lunch he was standing at Marcus's table with his tray, asking if they could talk before practice.

Marcus listened with his arms folded, which Daniel decided to read as thinking rather than defensive, because he had to decide something. "Priya nearly dropped out of the team after what you wrote on her last section," Daniel said. "And I didn't touch my essay all weekend. So your feedback isn't working. That's not an insult, it's just what happened."

"You want me to sugarcoat it."

"I want the opposite. Keep every hard comment. But be specific, so I know what to do, and tell me whether you think I can actually do it." He'd thought about leaving the second part out, about just modeling it, but that felt like a trick. "There was a study, 2014, Yeager. Students revised more when the criticism came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. One sentence. That's the whole difference."

Marcus was quiet long enough that Daniel started stacking his tray. Then Marcus pulled out his phone, opened the shared document, and typed at the top of Daniel's essay, in the comment box, while Daniel watched: "These are hard notes because I think this argument is worth making properly. You have the material. Let's see the second draft." Below it, the old comments still sat there, every "awkward" intact.

"Delete the one that just says 'unclear' on page three," Marcus said, still typing. "Tell me what I meant."
